chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the joint Disabilities and Parks hearing and announces rules for testimony, devices, and decorum. The chair is then invited to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and gives procedural instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning everyone and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing on Committee on Disabilities jointly with Committee on Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, during today's hearing, no one may approach the DS.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to testify, please find Sergeant in Arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No food or drinks allowed.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please silence all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shahana Hanif identifies herself as chair of the Disabilities Committee and welcomes attendees to the joint oversight hearing with Parks and Recreation. She thanks Parks Chair Ty Hankerson for joining.
chapters.title: Chair Hanif opens joint disabilities and parks oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shahana Hanif, Chair of the Committee on Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm a brown woman wearing glasses in my mid-30s with long black hair, and I'm seated behind a dais.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Welcome to today's joint oversight hearing with the Committee on Parks and Recreation on the accessibility of city parks, playgrounds, and recreation centers.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to my colleague, Parks Chair Ty Hankerson, for joining us for this important hearing.

chapters.summary: Hanif describes the 1984 Playground for All Children in Flushing Meadows Corona Park as a national model. She notes that the Parks Department did not finalize its ADA transition plan until June 2024, more than 30 years late.
chapters.title: Hanif recounts Playground for All Children and missed ADA deadlines

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In 1984, New York City opened the Playground for All Children in Flushing Meadows Corona Park.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It was the first playground in the country built so that children with and without disabilities could play together.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or the ADA, the city must make every park program and service accessible, even when the facility was built long before the law.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Federal rules gave the Department of Parks and Recreation until July 1992 to

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: come up with a plan for fixing its facilities and until January 1995 to finish the work.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The Parks Department didn't finalize its ADA transition plan until June 2024.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's more than 30 years late.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the transition plan leaves many questions unanswered, including that only 908 of 1,016 playgrounds have desired accessibility features. She notes fewer than half of restroom buildings, recreation centers, and pools have been fully evaluated.
chapters.title: Hanif details transition plan gaps in playgrounds, restrooms, rec centers, pools

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The transition plan is a start, but it leaves a lot unanswered.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It says 908 of the city's 1,016 playgrounds have the accessibility features that the Parks Department wants, which is not the same as saying they meet federal standards.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The Parks Department has fully evaluated 175 of its 622 public restroom buildings,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: 17 of the 36 recreation centers it operated at the time, and 11 of its 48 pools.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In each category, that is fewer than half.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And to reiterate, federal rules set a deadline to finish this work nearly 30 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But the transition plan doesn't set one at all.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the state comptroller found that 64% of observed barriers remained uncorrected 12 or more years after identification. She also notes auditors found the transition plan missing required elements and that the Parks website listed only 22 of 63 accessible facilities as accessible.
chapters.title: Hanif cites state comptroller findings on uncorrected barriers and inaccurate website

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The state comptroller has raised the same concerns.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In 2023, auditors found that 64% of the barriers they observed...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Remain uncorrected 12 or more years after the Parks Department first identified them.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In 2024, they found that the transition plan was missing every element federal rules require.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: list of barriers, how each will be fixed, a year-by-year schedule, and the official responsible.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Auditors also visited 85 facilities and found 63 of them accessible, but the Parks Department website listed only 22 as accessible.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When the parent of a child who uses a wheelchair is deciding whether to make the trip, incorrect information presents another barrier.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the U.S. Attorney's Office sued the Parks Department and Historic House Trust over the inaccessible Van Cortlandt House Museum. She notes the parties settled in February and agreed to make the museum accessible within five years.
chapters.title: Hanif describes federal lawsuit over Van Cortlandt House Museum accessibility

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When these barriers go unaddressed, the federal government can step in.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In June 2024, the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York found that the Van Cortlandt House Museum, the oldest standing building in the Bronx, was not accessible to visitors with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The U.S.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Attorney's Office sued the Parks Department.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And the Historic House Trust the following year.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This past February, the parties settled, and the Parks Department and the Historic House Trust agreed to make the museum accessible within five years.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It should not take a federal lawsuit, site by site, to make the city's parks accessible.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the committees want to learn how Parks will bring older facilities into compliance and add milestones to its transition plan. She expresses disappointment that the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities will not provide formal testimony.
chapters.title: Hanif outlines hearing questions and criticizes MOPD for not giving formal testimony

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: At this hearing, the committees are interested in learning how the Parks Department plans to bring its older facilities into compliance, including those without a planned capital project,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: when the Parks Department will add a schedule and year-by-year milestones to its transition plan,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How the Parks Department is responding to the Comptroller's findings on uncorrected

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: corrected barriers, inaccurate website information, and monitoring of concessionaires, and how the Parks Department and the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities work together to get this done.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I also want to express my disappointment that the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities will not be providing a formal testimony at today's hearing and will instead be available to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: As the city's lead office coordinating disability accessibility across agencies, MOPD has an important responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: To ensure that our parks, playgrounds, and recreation centers are accessible to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: While I appreciate their presence today, I believe their role warrants formal testimony and a public accounting of how they are working with the Parks Department to address longstanding accessibility barriers.

chapters.summary: Hanif says New York City built a model playground 42 years ago and today every park, playground, and recreation center should live up to that promise. She then passes the mic to Chair Hankerson.
chapters.title: Hanif calls for every park to live up to Playground for All Children promise

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: 42 years ago, New York City built a playground that became a model for the rest of the country.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Today, we want every park, playground, and recreation center in the five boroughs to live up to the promise of that playground for all children.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Before turning to the legislation, I'd like to pass the mic to Chair Hankerson for his opening statement.

chapters.summary: Parks Chair Ty Hankerson thanks Hanif for the joint hearing and describes growing up with a physical disability. He says parks and all park facilities should be accessible to all New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Chair Hankerson opens with personal disability experience and parks accessibility importance

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I am Ty Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I am a black man with a short haircut and a gray suit.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm chair of the Council's Committee on Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'd like to thank my colleague, Chair Hanif, for holding this hearing jointly with the Parks Committee.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It is now an often repeated claim by government officials, park advocates, and everyday citizens alike that the parks and playgrounds of our city are a critical part of our infrastructure and a vital service to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If that is the case, then it is obvious that parks and all facilities that make up the park system should be accessible to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This is a topic that is near and dear to me as someone who was born with a physical disability, having to wear braces for the first few years of my life and learning to walk.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Over the last few decades, the Parks Department has attempted to live up to that ideal.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: With, for example, the creation of accessible facilities such as the playgrounds for all children and the carousel for all children in the early 1980s.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: To the adaptive hubs and recreation centers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But in terms of full accessibility, it has largely fallen short in many ways since the passage of the ADA in 1990.

chapters.summary: Hankerson outlines ADA requirements that local governments remove architectural and communication barriers where readily achievable. He notes the Department of Justice published revised Title II and III regulations in 2010.
chapters.title: Hankerson explains ADA barrier removal and 2010 DOJ standards

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As Chair Hanif just stated, the city must take measures to make all park facilities accessible under the ADA, no matter when such facilities were built.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Specifically, the laws require that local governments must remove architectural and communication barriers that are structural in nature, where such removal is readily achievable.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In cases where removal is not readily achievable, accommodations must be made available through alternative methods.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In 2010, the Department of Justice published revised regulations for Titles II and III of the ADA.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It set up minimum requirements for newly designed, constructed, or altered local government facilities and other public accommodations so that they are accessible by individuals with disabilities.

chapters.summary: Hankerson says a 2005 state comptroller audit and 2007 follow-up found many park facilities remained inaccessible even after renovations. The audits also found missing signage, inadequate information, and no formal complaint process.
chapters.title: Hankerson reviews 2005 and 2007 audits finding persistent accessibility gaps

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: When we look at the Parks Department's historical efforts regarding accessibility, it is a bit underwhelming to say the least.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: For example, a 2005 audit by the State Comptroller's Office and a 2007 follow-up found that while many of the park's existing facilities had been upgraded to improve accessibility,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: many of the department's other park facilities were not accessible even after the renovations.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It found that numerous facilities lacked on-site signage and other information regarding accessible sites,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: that the department had not provided adequate information on how to find facilities that meet ADA requirements, and that parks did not have required formal process to investigate complaints about accessibility issues, among others.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It recommended the Parks Department develop a transition plan to achieve ADA-compliant operations at each park facility, ensure that ADA compliance was incorporated into all

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: new and major alteration projects, and establish written guidelines for major alteration work that specify which projects must include ADA-compliant components.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: That was all from a 2005 audit.

chapters.summary: Hankerson emphasizes that nearly 20 years later, the 2023 state comptroller audit and 2024 follow-up found very similar issues. He says Parks neglected to fix barriers, excluded features from surveys, and did not adequately monitor concessionaires.
chapters.title: Hankerson notes 2023 and 2024 audits found same accessibility issues

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Chair Hanif touched on this earlier, but I'd like to emphasize the fact that another audit, almost 20 years,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: years later found very similar issues.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: 20 years later, similar issues.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The 2023 State Comptroller Audit and 2024 follow-up noted that parks neglected to fix numerous barriers identified by the audit that the department itself determined to be correctable in a readily achievable or achievable manner.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Parks also excluded numerous parks features from its accessibility survey, did not adequately monitor compliance with accessibility standards by its concessionaires,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: inaccurately displayed accessibility signage, and focused its efforts on ensuring new capital projects were ADA compliant rather than upgrading older and existing facilities to achieve compliance.

chapters.summary: Hankerson acknowledges Parks has cited resource constraints and that the Council has pushed for more parks funding. He says constraints cannot fully explain why Parks has not proactively addressed longstanding accessibility gaps.
chapters.title: Hankerson says resource constraints don't fully explain lack of proactive accessibility work

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Parks has often cited numerous resource constraints as being a major reason why the park system has yet to achieve full accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And that is a valid point.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This committee and the council as a whole have been strong advocates of pushing to increase the parks budget.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And we achieved some success this year.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Despite there being a long road to achieve the funding level that is truly needed, though.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: However, resource constraints cannot fully explain why after decades of shedding light on the very same accessibility gaps,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Parks has not taken the initiative internally to proactively get in front of the numerous barriers that many disabled New Yorkers still face.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Though the department's intent is good and progress has been made, its results are still lacking.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And it remains unclear as to what the ongoing status is regarding full accessibility in park facilities.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: We need to obtain a detailed account of what is actually going on with accessibility at park facilities so we can properly assess them and work together to address the deficiencies that still exist.

chapters.summary: Hankerson says the bills under consideration are a strong step toward better understanding and addressing park accessibility deficiencies. He thanks Chair Hanif.
chapters.title: Hankerson says bills are strong step toward park accessibility

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I believe the bills we are considering today are a strong step in that direction.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I look forward to examining them and the broader issue of park accessibility in greater depth today.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the hearing covers four pieces of legislation and begins with Intro 212, introduced at the request of Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso. The bill would require annual assessments of park entrances, bathrooms, playgrounds, beaches, and pools, plus timelines and a public map.
chapters.title: Hanif introduces Intro 212 requiring annual ADA compliance report and public map

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Today we are hearing four pieces of legislation, and we look forward to the administration's and the public's feedback on them.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: First, introduction number 212, my bill introduced at the request of Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: in relation to an annual report on compliance with the ADA standards for accessible design by the Department of Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If passed, it would replace the city's current parks accessibility report with an annual assessment of every park's entrances, bathrooms, playgrounds, beaches, and pools,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: a timeline for fixing whatever doesn't comply, and a public map.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: New Yorkers should be able to find out before they leave home whether they can access a particular park facility.

chapters.summary: Hanif introduces Intro 1177, sponsored by Council Members Lynn Shulman and Mercedes Narcisse, to require reduced admission fees for seniors, young adults, military members, veterans, their minor children, and people with disabilities. She reads Shulman's remarks supporting affordability and access.
chapters.title: Hanif presents Intro 1177 on reduced admission fees and reads Shulman remarks

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Next, intro number 1177, sponsored by Council Members Lynn Shulman and Mercedes Narcisse in relation to...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: requiring the Department of Parks and Recreation to charge senior citizens, young adults, active members of the military, veterans and their minor children, and persons with disabilities reduced admission fees to recreational facilities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd now like to read Councilmember Shulman's remarks on her bill.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Today, I'm proud to speak about my bill, Intro 1177, that will make New York City's parks and recreational facilities more affordable and accessible to the people who need them.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Our parks, recreation centers, zoos, museums, and botanical gardens are important public resources.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: They provide opportunities for recreation, education, and community engagement, but the cost of admission can create barriers for many New Yorkers and their families.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: My legislation, Intro 1177, aims to address these barriers by requiring the Department of Parks and Recreation to offer reduced admission fees to seniors, young adults, people with disabilities, active duty military personnel,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: veterans, and their minor children.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: At all parks, recreational facilities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The legislation would also expand the city's existing reduced annual membership fee program to include active duty military personnel and the minor children of veterans and active duty service members.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Those who are most vulnerable are the most affected by affordability.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This bill will help ensure that the city's public recreational and cultural resources

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: are within reach for all New Yorkers, especially seniors, people with disabilities, and our veteran families.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, and I look forward to working with my colleagues to advance this legislation.

chapters.summary: Hanif introduces Intro 1193, sponsored by Council Member Christopher Marte, to increase accessible swings in playgrounds. Marte says the bill would require at least two accessible swings in all city parks by 2036 and argues true accessibility means more than the ADA minimum.
chapters.title: Marte advocates for Intro 1193 requiring accessible swings in playgrounds

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Next, we have intro number 1193, sponsored by Councilmember Christopher Marte, in relation to increasing the availability of accessible swings in playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I will pass the mic to Councilmember Marte to share some remarks on his bill.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hanif and Chair Hankerson, for holding today's important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I'm here today to speak about my bill, Intro 1193, which will require the Parks Department to install at least two accessible swings in all New York City parks by 2036.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: While progress has been made to include more accessible play features throughout our playgrounds, true accessibility in parks is severely behind.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Currently, a park can be listed as having an accessible play feature on the Parks Department map, but this can mean as little as the benches in the park having back and armrest.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: While this may check a box to be in compliance with ADA for the children with disabilities who just want to be a kid and play with their friends, this is exclusion.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It is as if we're telling these kids that they matter less.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: If our public spaces can't be used by everyone, then we need to fix our public spaces, plain and simple.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Accessibility means more than just the bare minimum of what the ADA requires.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: but making spaces actually inclusive.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We have playgrounds for all children model, but with only six citywide, there is a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Intro 1193 will help get us there, ensuring that no matter what park they go to, a disabled child will know that there is at least something for them to play with while there.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I look forward to today's hearing as we discuss this topic and look forward to working with my colleagues to pass this bill.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Happy Thanksgiving, everyone, and I kick it back to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Marte.

chapters.summary: Hanif introduces Resolution 721 honoring Becky Ogle, who died last month. She says Ogle helped build grassroots support for the ADA in 1990 and spent decades defending it.
chapters.title: Hanif honors Becky Ogle and disability rights legacy

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And lastly, we have Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: 721, which I am sponsoring, honoring the life and legacy of Becky Ogle, who died last month.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: She helped build a grassroots support that passed the ADA in 1990 and spent the decades that followed defending it.

chapters.summary: Hanif acknowledges colleagues, administration officials, advocates, service providers, and members of the public. She thanks committee staff including Sarah Sucher and Chloe Rivera.
chapters.title: Hanif acknowledges attendees and committee staff

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge my colleagues who have joined us, Councilmember Marte, Epstein, Hankerson, and Murano, and Sanchez on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to the administration for being here today and to the advocates, service providers, and members of the public who have come to testify or submitted written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Your presence here is an act of self-advocacy, and we do not take it for granted.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you to the committee staff who made today's hearing possible, including Senior Legislative Counsel Sarah Sucher and Senior Legislative Policy Analyst Chloe Rivera.

chapters.summary: Committee counsel asks administration witnesses to raise their right hands and affirm they will tell the truth. The witnesses respond and are told they may begin testimony.
chapters.title: Committee counsel administers oath to administration witnesses

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Now the committee council would administer the oath to members of the administration prior to their testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Will you please raise your right hand and respond verbally with I do?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin testimony when ready.

chapters.summary: Ayanna Titus identifies herself as Assistant Commissioner for Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging at NYC Parks. She introduces colleagues from Parks and the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities.
chapters.title: Parks Assistant Commissioner Ayanna Titus introduces agency panel

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Good morning, my name is Ayanna Titus.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: I am a black woman wearing a pink jacket.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Hankerson, Chair Hannaf, members of the Parks Committee, members of the Disabilities Committee, and the members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Again, my name is Ayanna Titus, and I serve as Assistant Commissioner for Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging at NYC Parks.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: I'm joined today by Eric Bornstein, our Deputy Commissioner for Capital Projects, Rain Credo, our DEIB Project Coordinator who serves as the agency's Disabilities Service Facilitator,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Matt Drury, our Chief of Citywide Legislative Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We are also joined by our colleagues at the mayor's office for people.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sorry, Ayanna, do you mind bringing the mic closer to your lips or mouth, rather?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Is this better?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Much better.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We are also joined by our colleagues at the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, including

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Balkeese Mehering, the Deputy Commissioner and Senior Legal Officer, and James Irvin, the Senior Director of Physical Accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We are pleased to be here to offer an update on New York City's parks approach to improving accessibility of our facilities and programming with the goal of creating an inclusive park system for all.

chapters.summary: Titus says NYC Parks stewards over 30,000 acres, 14% of the city's landmass, and more than 5,000 properties. She lists 1,000 playgrounds, 14 miles of beaches, 66 pools, and dozens of recreation and nature centers.
chapters.title: Titus describes Parks mission and vast portfolio

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: In accordance with our agency mission to grow, maintain, and program a multifaceted system of parks, recreation facilities,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: natural areas, programs, and activations that enrich and enhance the lives of every New Yorker, New York City Parks serves as the steward of over 30,000 acres of land,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: 14% of New York City's landmass, caring for over 5,000 individual properties, including 1,000 playgrounds, 14

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: miles of public beaches, 66 pools, and dozens of recreation centers and nature centers.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: New York City Parks strives to help

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: All New Yorkers discover how New York City parks can enrich their lives, promoting physical and emotional well-being, and providing venues for fitness and peaceful respite for the widest possible audience.

chapters.summary: Titus says Parks has made great strides since the ADA passed in 1990 but acknowledges considerable work remains. She says accessibility is a central pillar of the agency's mission.
chapters.title: Titus says Parks has made strides but more work needed on accessibility

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Since the passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990, New York City Parks has made great strides in moving toward a fully accessible park system.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: But we acknowledge there is considerable more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Accessibility is a central pillar of New York City's Parks mission, and throughout all agency processes, we emphasize accessibility as a key consideration,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: looking to increase access throughout the facilities and programming cared for and managed by our agency to provide equal access system-wide for our patrons, partners, and employees with dignity and respect.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: This commitment is reflected through numerous efforts undertaken by the agency.

chapters.summary: Titus describes how Parks designers work with an accessibility coordinator to identify and remove barriers. She says pathways prioritize slopes under 5%, stairs are limited, and buildings include ramps, lifts, elevators, and accessible common areas.
chapters.title: Titus details accessible design practices for parks and buildings

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: While designing new park facilities or reconstructing existing facilities, our project designers in our capital division work closely with our accessibility coordinator

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: to implement policies and procedures to identify and remove existing barriers,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: ensuring ADA compliance in design and construction, and promoting a safe, accessible environment for everyone visiting a city park.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: As we implement physical improvements to key community resources like playgrounds, public restroom buildings,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: ball fields, recreation centers, and pools, we collaborate closely with area residents in the design of their parks reconstruction so that accessibility concerns can be prioritized

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: and the community needs can be met.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The landscape architects working on our exterior site projects aim to make each site as accessible as possible.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Pathways are designed to prioritize slope walkways with less than 5% grade, minimizing the use of ramps.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Stairs are limited to secondary pathways and only in conditions where necessary because of existing topographic conditions.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Our standardized accessible site furnishings include tables, chairs, drinking fountains, and bottle fillers, and we have adopted best practices that allow us to preserve site accessibility

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: that can be sustainably maintained, considering not only the site conditions follow construction, but also the accessibility of materials as they age over time.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: For the children's play equipment within our playgrounds, we strive to exceed ADA standards and have worked with manufacturers to create innovative, new, engaging, and accessible components that can be

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: enjoyed by children of all abilities.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: For example, we recently broke ground on a capital project to reconstruct Rupert Park in Manhattan

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: with a completely reimagined design that will create a park experience that celebrates the site's natural features while improving access for visitors of all ages and abilities.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The project will create connected ADA accessible routes throughout the park and combine adventurous play equipment with accessible pathways and striking views of the park's landscape.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The architects that design our park buildings start all projects with a detailed survey to identify any accessibility issues requiring reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Designs include ramps, lifts, and elevators with the proper clearances and fixture locations, mountings, and fixture types to bring all facilities into alignment with ADA design standards.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The designers ensure that all common areas, such as lobbies, restrooms, locker rooms, and offices, will meet accessibility standards required by the ADA in the most equitable way possible.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And we aim to provide hearing loops in any projects that include large instruction areas, such as large fit.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: areas, large computer labs, or large classrooms to provide this accommodation to our deaf and deaf or hard of hearing patrons.

chapters.summary: Titus cites recent accessible facilities including the Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center in Brooklyn, Lost Battalion Hall in Queens, and St. Mary's Recreation Center in the Bronx. She says Parks has invested over $5.35 billion in capital projects over the past decade.
chapters.title: Titus highlights Shirley Chisholm, Lost Battalion Hall, St. Mary's rec centers

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: To point out some recent examples, earlier this year, we opened the Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: in East Flatbush, Brooklyn, a brand new state-of-the-art facility incorporating the highest design standards for accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Just last month, we reopened Lost Battalion Hall Recreation Center in Regal Park, Queens.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The renovated building now offers accessible restrooms on every floor as well as wider and safer routes throughout the facility.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We recently reopened St.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Mary's Recreation Center in the Bronx with a new elevator, providing ADA access to the upper floors and wider door frames throughout the building,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: making it easier for visitors of all abilities to navigate the center.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Every single facility that we build or reconstruct is an investment in improving accessibility, and New York City Parks has invested over $5.35

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: billion in capital projects over the past decade, an average of over $500 million for facility improvements per year, providing accessibility improvements to parks all across the city.

chapters.summary: Titus says accessibility is complex and many parks were built before the ADA. She notes steep terrain and historic facilities can make full compliance structurally impractical, but Parks seeks to meet or exceed standards where possible.
chapters.title: Titus acknowledges older facilities and site limitations complicate full ADA compliance

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Of course, accessibility is a complex and

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: multifaceted concept, meaning different things to different people, and it can be a challenge

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: to broadly characterize the accessibility of a park system that includes thousands of sites, each of which hosts a wide range of amenities and features.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: In addition to providing accessibility improvements alongside with other site repairs on project-by-project basis, the agency has undertaken an effort to assess and quantify capital needs

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: within various types of assets throughout our portfolio, like playgrounds and restrooms, to develop a more comprehensive evaluation

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: of the state of good repair of these facilities, including accessibility features as agency resources allow.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: It is important to note that our extensive portfolio contains a widely diverse range of properties and facilities,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: many built prior to the enactment of the ADA and which may not be fully compliant with the latest design standards, though most offer some accessible features or portions that are accessible.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Many parks have widely varying topography and steep terrain, making full compliance structurally impractical at some sites, and some of our historic facilities cannot be significantly modified without threatening

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: or destroying their historic.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: historical significance.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Despite these site-specific limitations, we still seek to meet or exceed ADA standards to the greatest extent possible.

chapters.summary: Titus lists inclusive programs such as adaptive swim, wheelchair basketball, sled hockey, and Movies Under the Stars. She says Parks provides mandatory disability etiquette training for staff who interact with the public.
chapters.title: Titus describes adaptive programming and disability etiquette training

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: New York City Parks offers a variety of inclusive and adaptive sports and recreational programs citywide throughout many of our recreation centers, such as Shape Up New York City,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: fitness classes, adaptive swim, media education workshops, sports like youth and adult wheelchair basketball, sled hockey, and others.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Our agency offers a wide variety of public programming, much of which includes inclusive or adaptive activities for persons with disabilities, such as family festivals and parks or our summer movie series,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Movies Under the Stars, many of which are held in accessible locations within large parks and playgrounds and with bathrooms on sites.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The outdoor programs led by our urban park rangers like nature exploration walks

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: and historic and cultural programs are often hosted at accessible locations, though some programs do have physical limitations due to the terrain of New York City's natural areas.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: As many of our employees interact directly with the public every day, we provide training for staff on disability etiquette.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And promote awareness of best practice.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: practices and in city policies regarding accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: These educational opportunities, much of which is mandatory, ensure that parkies are performing their duties and interacting with individuals in a way that is respectful, inclusive, and free from discrimination.

chapters.summary: Titus says Parks provides reasonable accommodations with three days' notice and offers sign language interpretation, assistive listening devices, and closed captioning. She says digital content uses alt text and accessible document standards.
chapters.title: Titus outlines accessible communication and digital content efforts

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Of course, this commitment to accessibility is only meaningful if we can effectively communicate with New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So we work hard to ensure that people with disabilities can receive and convey information related to our programs and facilities in a manner that is accessible and consistent with their preferred communication methods.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: For public events hosted by the agency, reasonable accommodations can be made with three days notice by using the contact information located at the bottom of every event flyer in accordance with local law

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And we use established methods for providing in-person sign language interpretation, assistive listening devices, and closed captioning of videos when requested.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Our agency's digital content is accessible to and usable by people with disabilities thanks to the effort.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Efforts of our digital media and content strategy teams as they continually improve the user experience for everyone applying the relevant accessibility standards.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: For example, all images that are used on our website and social media posts are assigned meaningful alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: text descriptions which convey the information and purpose of the image with the use of programmatic alt text and the electronic documents made available on our websites follow the principles

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: of accessible document creation as outlined in accessible documents guide accessible PPT guide and accessible PDF guides developed by our colleagues at the mayor's office for people with disabilities

chapters.summary: Titus says Parks incorporates accessibility into workplace procedures and events. She says the agency promotes jobs to recruitment resources serving people with disabilities.
chapters.title: Titus notes workplace inclusion and recruitment efforts

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Lastly, our commitment to accessibility is reflected through many efforts to preserve, expand workplace inclusion

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: in compliance with the city's EEO policy as we incorporate accessibility into our workplace procedures and events and promote

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: our jobs to diverse recruitment resources, including those that serve people with disabilities.

chapters.summary: Titus says Intro 212 would repeal Local Law 73 reporting and require annual assessments of every park facility. She says the proposed scope far exceeds agency capacity and would divert staff from active capital projects.
chapters.title: Titus raises capacity concerns with Intro 212 reporting mandate

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Turning to the legislation formerly being considered today, Introduction 212 would repeal an existing reporting requirement regarding

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: park accessibility previously mandated by Local Law 73 of 2015 and require a new annual assessment of every park under the agency's jurisdiction to determine if each facility

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: in such park conforms to applicable federal, state, and local accessible design standards.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We share the council's support for openness and transparency, and we appreciate

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: the importance of continuing to monitor and assess the accessibility of our park system.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Our agency website provides up-to-date information about the wide range of facilities, programming, and services offered by New York City Parks, including accessibility of facility amenities,

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: scheduled programming, and other opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: However, we have significant concerns about the legislation as it is currently drafted, as the proposed scope of the reporting that would be mandated far exceeds the agency's

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: current capacity and resources.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: It should be noted that existing reporting rubric for Local Law 73 is already a significant undertaking for our agency staff, and legislatively mandating more comprehensive reporting requirements

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: would divert staff time and energy away from managing the active capital projects that are delivering substantive improvements in parks.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Accessibility for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Titus says Intro 1193 would require two accessible swings in half of playgrounds by 2033 and all remaining playgrounds by 2036. She says Parks typically includes accessible swings in playground renovations and nearly half of swing-set playgrounds already have them, but the bill raises operational concerns.
chapters.title: Titus discusses accessible swings and concerns with Intro 1193

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Introduction 1193 would require the installation of at least two accessible swings in half of the playgrounds under Parks jurisdiction by 2033

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: and in every remaining playground under our jurisdiction in 2036.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We very much share the council's support for inclusive play equipment for children of all abilities to enjoy.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: When a capital project will construct or renovate a children's playground featuring a swing set, we typically incorporate accessible swings, and they are very popular with little park goers.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Approximately 900 of our park playgrounds feature swing sets, nearly half of which currently offer accessible swings, and we are increasing this number at every available opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The legislation as it is currently drafted raises some operational and logistical concerns, but we would be happy to take part

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: in further conversations with the council regarding both introduction 1193 and introduction

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: 212 to identify potential alternative approaches to best achieve our shared goal of ensuring the most accessible park system possible.

chapters.summary: Titus says Intro 1177 would add active military members to those eligible for reduced recreation center admission. She notes veterans, seniors, and people with disabilities already pay $25 annually and says Parks appreciates the bill's intent.
chapters.title: Titus supports intent of Intro 1177 on reduced fees for active military

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Introduction 1177 would add active members of the military or reserve armed forces to the universe of individuals that are eligible for reduced admission to New York City Parks Recreation Centers.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: In line with Mayor Mondami's vision for a more affordable city, we are very proud to be the agency of affordability because parks are for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: In a city where a gym membership can cost you hundreds of dollars for every month, we provide completely free.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: free or low-cost access to our recreation centers that every New Yorker can enjoy.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Kids and young adults under 25 are always eligible for year-round recreation center memberships completely for free at no charge whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Citywide membership

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Memberships for adults age 25 to 61 are typically $150 for an entire year with an additional 10% discount for anyone with the IDNYC card.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Military veterans, seniors, and people with disabilities are eligible for annual memberships costing only $25.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We very much appreciate the intent of this bill and agree that actively serving

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: members of our military should be entitled to enjoy the incredible benefits of our recreation centers at the most affordable rate possible.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing this legislation further with the council in consultation with our colleagues at the Mayor's Office of Management and Budget and Department of Veteran Services.

chapters.summary: Titus thanks the committees for the opportunity to testify and says Parks looks forward to continuing the conversation on park accessibility. She offers to answer questions.
chapters.title: Titus closes Parks testimony and offers to answer questions

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We have appreciated the opportunity to testify today and look forward to continuing the important conversation.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Conversation about improving park accessibility across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We thank you for your continued advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: and support for our city parks and would now be happy to answer any questions that you have.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify that we're joined by Councilmember Piarina Sanchez on Zoom and we

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Also have council members Joseph, Nurse, and Ung here with us today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you for the comprehensive testimony.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks who serves as Parks' ADA coordinator and where the role sits in the agency. Matt Drury distinguishes the capital-division ADA coordinator from disability service facilitators in the DEIB division.
chapters.title: Hanif asks Parks about ADA coordinator's role and reporting structure

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to kick off by asking about Parks'ADA coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share who that is and where does that role sit in the agency's org chart and to whom does that person report?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: My name's Matt Drury, white male, brown hair, wearing a gray suit.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'm the Chief of Citywide Legislative Affairs for the agency.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: To clarify, just because an ADA coordinator, we have a specific staffer that

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: sits within our capital division and we can talk a little bit about the work that individual does with that with our capital design team we also have disability service facilitators

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: within the agency two of which signed within our DEIB division so I guess just could you share about both yeah yeah sure so we'll start with the disability service facilitators first

chapters.summary: Ayanna Titus says the agency has two disability service facilitators, Rain Credo and Rodolfo Guevara, who handle complaints and reasonable accommodation requests. She confirms the disability services role is not a full-time portfolio and includes other DEI work.
chapters.title: Parks says disability service facilitators split time across DEI duties

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So currently the agency has two disability services facilitators, one of which is Rain Credo right here, and the other is Rodolfo Guevara, who are situated in my division.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: A lot of what they do is work with people with disabilities who have complaints, who make requests for reasonable accommodations.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: They also work with training and coordinate with MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: They typically are working hand in hand, I would say, with MOPD, especially because the disability service facilitators meet sort of on a regular basis with MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: I would say those are sort of the general duties of the disability services facilitators.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And then I'll turn it over to my colleague to talk a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Before you turn it over to your colleague.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So the disability services coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is more constituent facing?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The facilitator is a little bit more constituent facing in terms of addressing requests for reasonable accommodations or complaints and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how are those requests and complaints coming in?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So they can come in a variety of ways.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Sometimes it's through 311, but we also on our website have a specific email address where a constituent could email the disability services facilitator directly.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And that comes to RAINN, and then RAINN would address the issue.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then is the DSF?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: also doing other parks, serving other parks roles, or is that the primary role of the disability services facilitator?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So within my division, the two disability service facilitators do other aspects related to DEI type of work.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share more about that?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So sometimes what we have is programming that they might be responsible for that relates to DEI that can include people with disabilities and other sort of protected groups that we might be discussing.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: They might be working also on training.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So, for instance, we have gender identity type of training.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So RAINN is also assisting with that.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We also have programs related to what we call restorative practices, where we would be talking about a variety of issues.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We have a newsletter.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So there's other types of duties that they also are responsible for.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So just to be clear, the disability services component is not the full-time portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It is one part of a larger DEI type.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: I would have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And part of this is, again, we have very limited staff and we are kind of stretched in terms of the amount, I would say, the work and the things that we are responsible for.

chapters.summary: Rain Credo says the DSF tracks requests and complaints in an Excel spreadsheet, including complaint type, referral, and resolution status. Credo estimates the office receives about 20 to 50 requests per year.
chapters.title: Parks says DSF logs 20-50 accommodation requests yearly in Excel

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then what per month or quarter?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: kind of tracking is being done to log how many folks with disabilities were contacted, issues resolved, or

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: complaints filed with

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: CCHR or referred to MOP-D, what's being logged?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Okay, so yes, we do track complaints and we do maintain them on an Excel spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Let Rain talk a little bit more about the work that they do in terms of tracking.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: My name is Rain Criddle.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: I am a black, non-binary human.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: I am wearing a black dress, and I have black hair.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: As the Disability Services Facilitator for Parks, we receive requests and complaints through our email, through phone,

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: and through our, we have a page where people can request accommodations as well.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: So we have a variety of ways in which we receive information and feedback from our constituents.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: And generally, I take that information down on an Excel spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, could you repeat the question again?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wanted to understand how we're keeping a log or track of constituents with disabilities who are

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: reaching out.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Yeah, so it's generally through this Excel spreadsheet that I have where I take information, I take their name, what the complaint is, who will I forward the complaint to,

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: if the complaint is resolved or not, what type of complaint it is, or, you know, request that it is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And are you able to share

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: maybe per month, how many of these kinds of complaints or outreach you're getting?

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: That's a really good question.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: We don't really do it by month, but I would say by year.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Rain could probably speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Yes, so by year, we get anywhere from like,

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: 20, 25 to 50 requests.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: And again, they are all recorded through our Excel sheet.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, so per year, 20.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Give or take.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Give or take 20 requests.

utterances.text: Would you say that the disability services facilitator is a position that New Yorkers know about?

utterances.text: I think there's a lot to be done in terms of general cultural education, disability awareness writ large.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of the specific, and my understanding is most, if not all, city agencies have similar positions, how widespread that knowledge is, it's kind of hard for us to speak to, except to note that, you know,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In general, I'd characterize that your average New Yorker probably isn't super familiar with the intricacies of agency staffing or governmental staffing writ large, including, but not limited to, the disability services.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I only ask that because 20 is surprising.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You know, on a regular basis, our council offices are getting dozens of...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Complaints and outreach about specific parks, playgrounds related concerns.

chapters.summary: Eric Bornstein says Edmund Asidu is the capital division's ADA coordinator. He says Asidu participates in site assessments, community engagement, design review, and construction inspections for capital projects.
chapters.title: Eric Bornstein describes ADA coordinator Edmund Asidu's capital project role

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, so moving on to the ADA coordinator, could you tell me a little bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: My name is Eric Borsten.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Commissioner for Capital Projects and Parks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'm a white male wearing glasses and a gray suit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So for the Capital Division, our Disability Coordinator is Mr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Edmund Asidu.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He's with us this morning, present this morning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And Edmund's responsibilities include participating in any capital project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: within our portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He would typically participate in our team's early assessment of sites.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And this is, to be clear, once a project is deemed for a capital project, that's when my team would get involved.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We would do an assessment of the existing conditions of all conditions on the park, including accessibility with a lack thereof.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It would be part of that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Teams, efforts, we develop budgets for these projects, scopes of work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And when a project is fully funded and begins designed, Edmund participates in our community engagement meetings with the constituents at each park's community so that we can hear directly from them,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: the people who use the parks, the people who will be using the parks, what their hopes for that park renovation might be, what their specific needs might be, any particular issues.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Edmund then participates with every project's design as it evolves.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He reports to the chief of landscape design at Capitol and works with the chief and the chief staff to make sure that every design is designed to be fully compliant with the design standard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And then if that weren't enough, Eddie will visit construction sites and completed projects to make sure that the work as built by our contractors.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Is conforming with the design and is in compliance with the design standard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He's a young man.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether Eddie is the only coordinator and how large his team is. Bornstein says Eddie works by himself but serves as a resource to 450 capital staff who are trained in accessibility guidelines.
chapters.title: Bornstein says ADA coordinator works alone but supports trained capital staff

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is Eddie the only coordinator within the capital portfolio?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so he is tasked with assessing...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: ADA related inquiries or design.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: You know, Eddie leads the team, but every member of the capital staff, architects, landscape architects, all of them are trained to be familiar with, really experts in accessibility guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: When we do in-house design work, they are responsible for making sure their designs are compliant.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And Eddie serves as a resource to them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He's not by far the only one who is concerned with these issues, but he's a resource if there's a question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Sometimes the accessibility guidelines are hard to interpret.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Sometimes there are gray areas between interpretation of what the letter of the law says, the letter, the actual written content of the design standard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It is a resource to those designers and to our private sector consultants who are also working on designs to make sure that if there's a decision to be made, it's a well-advised one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: If there's a choice to be made, we make the best choice we can.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: If there's a question about the applicability of a particular standard, we understand how best to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So, you know, while, yes, he is the only one with that title, the only one with that job description, I would like to say that everybody on the staff is

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: educated and expert enough in these requirements, as they are with the building code and safety standards and other comparable types of design standards to make sure their designs are compliant.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And then others are resident engineers, are consultant CMs, likewise, generally expert in this material.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We hire them on that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: basis and we train them so that really anybody can go to the site and identify a deficiency if something is built wrong,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: go to a site prior to the beginning of a project to identify an issue that needs to be addressed, and then look at a design, you know, a set of drawings as they're developed

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: and identify how any issues that were identified are designed to be remedied and that the design proposals are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Eddie, again, is a resource to the department.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: An educator, a trainer, an advisor, and an interpreter, far from the only one with this expertise.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how big is Eddie's team?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Eddie works by himself.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He has a team of one.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So when you were saying team,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Well, the design teams that work on projects will be several people.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So on a capital project, starting from leadership, myself on down to my assistant commissioners, my chiefs of design,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: the team leaders for every one of our landscape design studios, ultimately the landscape architects and engineers working on a project or the ones managing consultants, a project is developed by a team that could be quite large, depending on the size and scope of the project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It is a part of that team.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Participates in the project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: That's his role, again, but he doesn't himself manage a team of people doing this work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He's a part of the teams.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many full-time staff work on accessibility, compliance, surveys, and design review. Bornstein says all capital staff are conversant in accessibility standards and responsible for compliance in their projects.
chapters.title: Bornstein says all 450 capital staff handle accessibility compliance

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then how many full-time staff work on accessibility, including compliance, site surveys, and design review?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yeah, so, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I don't mean to be flippant about it, but really all

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: All of them do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So the capital team at Parks is 450 lines.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We have some vacancies, of course, but everybody on a project, everybody really within the program is, again, building code, energy code, safety requirements, ADA, all of these standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Conversant in them, knowledgeable of them, and works to make sure their designs are compliant.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So then could you clarify what is the ADA coordinator's role specifically if every 450 staff in the department is knowledgeable?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: knowledgeable, he's the one they go to with questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He's the one that can answer a question from a constituent.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He's the one who can look at design and answer the technical questions that perhaps rise above the ability of that staff.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What kind of questions?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: ADA, you know, the design standard is really a very meticulous document.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'm sure you're all very familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: For instance, in an existing park where we have existing topography and presuming as most of them might be the older parks designed and constructed long before the adoption of the design standard

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: wouldn't be compliant with this particular set of requirements requiring us to regrade to landscape to remove existing site stairs and replace them either with ramps.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Or with more gently gradient walkways and pathways to make sure we understand what areas need to be accessible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So that's called the accessible route to identify the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: to make sure all things, all features required to be on an accessible route are properly identified.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Eddie is the one we would go to if there's a question about interpretation, if it's a question about execution,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: if there are some gray areas, if there are some anomalies, if there's two different ways to solve a problem, which one is generally deemed to be better, more in compliance, more in compliance with the spirit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Of the law.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And then as things are designed in detail, the dimensions are extraordinarily meticulous, very, very specific with not much tolerance for construction tolerances.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And again, Eddie can inspect the site.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He can go to a site, perform an inspection at a high level to make sure that everything is built properly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So again, most of the staff, all the staff, familiar with, aware of, and knowledgeable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Eddie is the one expert they can always go to when a question exceeds their particular level of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It is still a little confusing, but maybe as we continue to learn during this hearing, I'll have a clearer understanding of.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
