utterances.text: The ADA coordinator's role.

chapters.summary: Hanif says the November 2024 comptroller follow-up found Parks had not developed formal ADA rules, policies, or defined the ADA coordinator's duties. Drury says he was not involved in the audit response and disagrees with the characterization.
chapters.title: Hanif cites comptroller finding Parks lacks formal ADA rules; Drury disagrees

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In its November 2024 follow-up, the state comptroller found that Parks still had not developed formal ADA rules, policies, and procedures, or defined the ADA coordinator's duties, and that Parks disagreed with the recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you say a little bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, thanks for your question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: To be frank, I'm not aware that anyone at this table was directly involved in that audit or the response to it.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So I think we're going to need to get a little more context, most likely in consultation with Parks Council and Corporation Council.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: You know, just as I don't believe we were directly involved in the...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So are you unable to say...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Anything about the fact that the department has not developed ADA rules, policies, or is that a false statement?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Or is this a false statement?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think we would differ with that notion.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think the agency has a very clear approach to accessibility, and as we testified, it's imbued within, essentially, we think it's at the core of our effort in terms of increasing access equitably for the park system writ large.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks where the public can read a formal description of the ADA coordinator's duties. Drury says detailed agency job descriptions are generally not publicly available outside job postings and agrees to look further.
chapters.title: Drury says ADA coordinator job description not publicly available

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then is there any place where we can read the formal description of the ADA coordinator's duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'm not aware that detailed job descriptions of any agency position are publicly available outside of the context of a job posting.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'm not aware that those are...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: robustly, you know, similar.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'm not aware that a committee council job description is posted anywhere publicly or a council member for that matter.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So I believe the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Happy to look further into that, but I'm not aware that it is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I would prefer that that be looked into so that this committee can have a

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: better understanding of the ADA coordinator's duties.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, perhaps attached to the civil service title description.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, I'm just trying to understand exactly what the coordinator does.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We're happy to do our best here.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You brought it up.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Council member, I'm happy to give you what I do.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: You know.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: You know.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I believe Commissioner Borsten provided actually a pretty robust description of what the– and I apologize if that isn't– I disagree.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Landing?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It's hard.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to actually understand the–

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: To me, it feels like the DSF and the ADA coordinator are roles that are being checked off as opposed to actually serving an actual accessibility

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: related portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we would differ strongly with that characterization.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I would like to be persuaded.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks who sits on the Parks ADA Advisory Committee and how members are chosen. Titus says the committee has been inactive since COVID and a lead staffer involved with it left the agency.
chapters.title: Parks says ADA Advisory Committee inactive since COVID

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share who sits on the Parks'ADA Advisory Committee?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how are members chosen, how often does it meet.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The only public comment on the five-year accessibility plan asked for more information about this committee.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: I'll just say in general, we do communicate with our disability advocates, but with respect to this ADA advisory committee, it has really been inactive since COVID.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And so we also had one of our lead

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: persons who was involved with the ADA advisory committee leave the agency.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So that's something that we definitely have to sort of get active again.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So this committee has been discontinued since COVID?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Inactive is the word I would use.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Yes, because we still talk with disability advocates, groups and whatnot, but we just haven't met.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So a lot of times we get contacted, RAINN has gotten contacted with...

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: From different constituents about issues, concerns, but my point was that we hadn't had a formalized sort of meeting since COVID regarding this specific- I mean, that's like six years.

chapters.summary: Drury gives an example of Parks engaging disability advocates on recreation center membership rules. Hanif asks for a timeline to reactivate the committee, and Drury says there is no timeline but it is under active discussion.
chapters.title: Parks says no timeline to reactivate ADA advisory committee

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'd like to add an anecdotal example that I think will help provide some context.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And actually, the Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities is an extremely helpful resource.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So last year,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: 2025, the agency, with the input from disability advocates, underwent an exercise to update our agency rules.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We had been getting feedback that the

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: types of documentation that were required to qualify for the recreation center membership were somewhat limiting.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And so the mayor's office of persons with disabilities and others kind of helped convene.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And some of these members, I think, had previously served in

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: the advisory committee when it was sort of formally constituted as such, but we were able to engage in some really helpful conversations and get some great feedback about alternative additional types of documentation that we were able to incorporate into our rules change.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And now, thankfully, a person with a disability can provide those additional.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So that's just one anecdotal example of how we are sort of engaging with

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: advocates and other members of the community at every available opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So is there a timeline to reactivate the committee?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I wouldn't say there's a timeline.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's under active, it's something we're discussing very actively.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Well, that's disappointing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, it's been about six years or so since COVID and that this is inactive.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And who within the department would be facilitating the committee?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is that the DSF?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Well, that's one of the pieces of consideration, just to provide some additional context.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The assignment of the disability service facilitators within DEIB is a relatively recent development that just took place, I believe, two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So we are in the process as an agency of updating, and that's, again, in coordination with the ADA coordinator and the capital staff in terms of physical improvements that are delivered through capital.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: the DEIB division kind of having a more holistic sort of view of our sort of inclusion efforts.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Like that is sort of a more recent transition that I think is still bearing itself out and getting fleshed out in a variety of different ways, including, but not limited to the advisory committee.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how Parks works with MOPD day to day and whether MOPD reviews capital designs. Bornstein says MOPD does not review projects as a matter of course, and MOPD's Balkeis Meherig describes site visits and feedback on projects like Bella Abzug Park and the Battery Playscape.
chapters.title: MOPD describes collaboration with Parks on capital projects and site visits

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how does Parks work with MOPD day to day?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Does MOPD review capital designs before construction, for example?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Typically not, but we collaborate with them whenever we find that their additional advice or insight into a project would be useful.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share some examples?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Well, I mean...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I could share.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yeah, could you please?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yeah, but a lot of war stories.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: My name is Balkeis Meherigam, the Deputy Commissioner and Senior Legal Officer for MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: I'm feeling a little unwell today, so if you need me to speak up, just let me know.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: I am a North African olive-skinned woman wearing a burgundy suit.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Parks collaborates fairly frequently with us in a variety of different ways.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Capital projects are not reviewed, as a matter of course, by MOPD because, as stated earlier by my colleagues, there are many accessibility experts on staff at Parks.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: However, they have reached out to us for feedback on certain occasions.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: For example, the design of Bella Abzug Park, we provided feedback there.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: I don't think this was a capital project.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Bella Abzug was a capital project, but the Ali Pond obstacle course, which I don't believe was an at-capital project, but MOPD did a site visit and visited that.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Parks frequently invites us and solicits our feedback on...

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: park redesigns and so we've had a couple of tours and site visits of various parks.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: The Battery Playscape is another example.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: We recently toured the Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center with Commissioner Shimamura, which was a beautiful facility.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: I encourage you all to attend if you haven't had a chance.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: There are sloped entries into the pool.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Every aspect of that rec center was designed with accessible features.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: And so those are, and not to mention, you know, we convene the DSFs on a monthly basis to discuss various constituent issues.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: And there are other variety of ways, but I'll answer the, I'm answering the question specific to designs and capital projects.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what kind of feedback MOPD provides and how often it convenes disability service facilitators. Meherig says MOPD convenes DSFs monthly with an agenda and provides practical feedback from people with disabilities during site visits.
chapters.title: MOPD says it convenes DSFs monthly and provides lived-experience feedback

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So the kind of feedback that you're sharing, could you articulate more clearly what kind of feedback that is?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then I'd also love to know how frequently is MOPD convening the DSFs and is there an agenda?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How do you all exchange?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Lessons and what's happening at those convenings?

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: I'll answer your last question first quickly.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: We convene them monthly and yes, there is an agenda and we share resources and updates, discuss issues that come up that DSFs have questions about.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Mike seems to be cutting out.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: With regards to physical accessibility feedback, when we do site visits, I'm accompanied today by the Senior Director of Physical Accessibility, James Irvin.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: We would attend site visits with James typically, as well as some of our staff with physical disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: And so, you know, as you were discussing earlier about the ADA, the ADA is a floor.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: And so there are questions and issues that come up that lived experience is really relevant and answers those questions.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Like what would be best?

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: How does a person with disabilities experience the space?

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: What kind of issues come up?

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: And so that very practical real life feedback is part of, you know, what we do in addition to ensuring that ADA requirements are met.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: And we also incorporate, you know, constituent feedback that we've heard over the years about certain, you know, access issues.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize you've been joined by Council Members Narcisse, Krishnan, and Lee.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to pass to Chair Hankerson for questions.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks what the transition plan means when it says 908 of 1,016 playgrounds have accessible site features. Drury and Bornstein say newer or reconstructed playgrounds generally meet 2010 standards, while older facilities vary.
chapters.title: Hankerson questions Parks on 908 accessible playgrounds and 2010 standards

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I have just a few questions concerning playgrounds and rec centers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The transition plan says that 908 out of 1,016 playgrounds have

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: all accessible site features we desire.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What exactly does that phrase cover?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, my recollection is that that phrasing was a reference to significant accessibility features being incorporated into a playground design, not limited, including but not limited to

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: ramps and other sort of accessible swings and other sort of accessible elements of that nature.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Would you say those features meet the 2010 standards?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Commissioner Borson can correct me.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think broadly speaking, any playground constructed or materially reconstructed following 2012 or so will absolutely meet the 2010 standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I would concur.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Any capital project, any park, playground, rec center, public restroom building constructed since the adoption of the design standards would be designed and constructed to fully comply.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Sometimes there are extenuating circumstances, sometimes there are minor deviations, but the intent and by and large the results suggest that we design and build those projects to comply.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Older facilities, of which, as we all know, there are many, would not be likely to comply.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And while we would go in with something less than a full-blown capital project and try to address obvious deficiencies that are readily

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: resolved, that would be an accessible feature that would be better than what was there before, but would be far short than full compliance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So I think it's a case-by-case basis, but I think, again, any project enacted subsequent to the adoption of the design standards, we would be very confident that full compliance is the goal and has been achieved.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Anything earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Accessibility would vary greatly site by site, but full compliance of something built prior to the adoption of the design standards would be unlikely to be in compliance.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether Parks sends inspectors to ensure compliance and whether park staff are trained in ADA. Drury describes a randomized parks inspection program and says day-to-day staff are likely not trained in granular ADA details.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks how Parks inspects playgrounds and trains staff on ADA

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Does Parks send out an inspector to ensure that...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: That the park or playground is in compliance?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Well, again, after a project is completed, part of our process of closeout and to make sure the contractors perform to work properly, there are many, many inspections scheduled throughout the course of a project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Likewise, during the design phase, many, many reviews to make sure the design hasn't missed something or makes an error or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We have a capital needs assessment team, a small team, tiny but mighty, that is assessing many of our parks facilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Their purview is far wider than simply ADA.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We recognize the value and the importance of ADA compliance, but their purview is to look at many things, structural stability, state of good repair, energy code, you know, does the roof leak, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Their purview is far broader, and so they will report on the conditions of their findings and say,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: you know, a rec center is not in compliance with the ADA and the boiler doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And so this becomes sort of the source of advocating for a future capital project.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So does that team or that unit perform regular inspections to ensure that a facility or a playground or a location

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: remains in compliance?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: They will, do you want to?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: No, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'll intercede here that in terms of day-to-day sort of observation in terms of a property, including an element that, you know,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: may be failing or, you know, no longer, and this could be as simple as sort of a raised, you know, sidewalk flag or what have you, that's typically handled by our, we have a lot of different ways for what you might call sort of routine park inspection.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That happens at the, you know, ground level with staff that's in our parks every day.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But most, I think the probably most emblematic version of that is our parks inspection program, which is a...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Secret shopper inspection program for lack of a better term that is independently conducted from our operations unit

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's it's our operations and management planning team and they end it and there's a team and they conduct up to 6,000 inspections every year and that is a much more exhaustive how often at a single park.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, no, no, that's okay It it does vary larger, but but that and this I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: This is a very rigorous comprehensive fairly exhaustive inspection that includes accessibility aspects, but it's not so, you know, that is not far also wider ranging than that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's 6,000 inspections a year.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So a typical parks property will be inspected two to three times a year.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I mean, it can vary, but because it's randomized, I should, I should mention that as well.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's sort of, and that's the intent.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So you primarily rely on your park staff that are there day to day.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, not to mention 311 requests.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: New Yorkers are not shy.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There's no shortage of incoming input we receive from a variety of sources.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but my only follow-up question to that would be, are all park staff trained in ADA compliance to be able to recognize if something is out of compliance during an inspection or a day-to-day routine operation?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: No, it's a good question and a fair one.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think the...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: ADA design standards are a fairly technical and exacting information realm.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I would argue that our parks inspection inspectors are definitely trained and a pressing concern at the risk of, I'm not minimizing it, but it's usually fairly apparent when it's, but in terms of whether day-to-day staff is,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: you know, highly trained in the, you know, granular details of ADA, you know, design standards, you know, likely not.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Understood.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks for a list with schedule and funding status for the 108 playgrounds not counted as having accessible features. Drury says the data is a snapshot from about two years ago and Parks will circle back.
chapters.title: Hankerson requests schedule and funding status for 108 playgrounds

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: For the other 108 playgrounds, will Parks give the committee a list with a schedule and funding status for each?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we can circle back to the data set that you're referencing there.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Again, this was a snapshot in time from two-ish years ago, so I think we're happy to take a closer look at that data set and circle back with that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What's the yearly repair budget, and how long does a damaged surface typically stay out of service?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So the agency's operational budget is really, is not segmented out by

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: asset like feature in quite that way.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We have both a capital budget for major reconstructions and our 10-year capital plan is eight something billion dollars.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's fairly considerable.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: 12, sorry, 12 billion dollars.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Underestimated.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And then we also have on the expense, what you might call the expense side, sort of, you know, as you're well aware, a

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: you know, a finite but, you know, significant budget.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I forget that annual budget, but repairs and, you know, we have dedicated trade staff, borough M&O maintenance and operations staff that is also making sort of day-to-day targeted repairs and fixes.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But I don't have a dollar figure because that's not the way the agency's budget is structured.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'll circle back to that because I do have a follow-up question, but I do want to get to the recreation centers.

chapters.summary: Hankerson notes the transition plan evaluated only 17 of 36 recreation centers and asks what the evaluations found. Drury says five of 37 rec centers lack an accessible route between floors, and two are slated for repair.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about rec center evaluations and accessible routes between floors

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The transition plan says Parks had comprehensively evaluated 17 of its 36 recreation centers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Parks now operates 37, including the Shirley Chisholm Recreation Center, which opened in February 2026.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What did those evaluations find, and when will the rest be completed?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Also, how many multi-story centers have no accessible route between floors?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I can take the second part first, and then in terms of the broader, in terms of characterizing the broader condition of our rec centers, I think Commissioner Borsten can help narrate that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I can confirm that of our 37 recreation centers, there are five that lack an accessible route between floors for the public.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Two of these five are slated for active repair.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's Al Smith in Manhattan and Owen Dolan in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Those two are...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: On the way.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Is that, was that selected by way of your inspection team?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And pardon me, I don't know the correct name.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: No, it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I, in terms of how our facilities and properties get designated for capital work, it can be inspired by a variety of different fashions.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The agency has undertook different approaches over the years to how to prioritize our investment.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And certainly,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I would argue that the age of a facility and its capital condition is a pretty core part of that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So when a property is in a severe state of disrepair, it is a higher priority for the agency.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But again, this is all pending the availability of funding.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So it's a bit of a moving target.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks how Parks prevents facilities from reaching severe disrepair instead of repeatedly seeking emergency capital funds. Drury says preventative maintenance is core but aging facilities and limited funding make it difficult.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks how Parks prevents facilities from falling into disrepair

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So I guess my question, and Commissioner, I'm going to come back to you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: How do we prevent our facilities from even getting to that point?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Instead of us having to come back years later and say we have to invest all this money into it, now we're pulling from this and that and that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: How do we prevent us from ever getting to that point?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Well, prevent is probably the best word there, and preventative maintenance is obviously a core feature of our staffing model.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We are, in many cases, some of our facilities are upwards of a century old.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Some of our pools and other facilities were works project administration projects, the New Deal projects, and there's no denying that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Even with every best effort in terms of daily preventative maintenance, time will take its toll, right?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That is sort of just things will reach the end of their useful life.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That is just a fact of the physical world we live in.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But having said that, I think we are committed.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It is very clear that preventative daily care and maintenance can extend the useful life of all of our parks, playgrounds, and other facilities in a long, long way.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Would you say that?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: care and maintenance is equitable across the city?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We're very committed to making sure that our parks and playgrounds are in the best condition possible across the city.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I think our parks inspection program, which is again sort of

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: randomized and sort of, you know, data blind in that sense, like that it, you know, that it is that it is going out and we're inspecting and assessing our properties randomly and equitably in that regard is, I think, one example.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Another example is our community parks initiative, which is where we're investing upwards of five, six, seven, eight million dollars in renovating and refreshing parks completely from scratch, usually redesigning them entirely.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And for those, we're prioritizing properties that haven't seen investment for 20 years or more.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And sad to report, not surprising though, many of those properties are in communities of color or other places where that, you know, have been, we believe, underserved over the decades.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Why would you say, why is that so?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Why is why are we prioritizing those properties?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: No, I know why you're prioritizing those properties, but you said these properties.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Why were they neglected?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Well, that I mean, that is an excellent.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I mean, maybe sociologists or, you know, I can't really speak to how or why are those things happen over time.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: All I know is that we're committed to, you know, correcting and redirecting and making sure I think this administration and this this agency is committed to equity.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's, you know, for us, it's not just lip service.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think, you know, I think we have a.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: A dedicated core, our commissioner, I think it's, you know, I think it's core to

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: her being, and I think it sort of imbues, you know, fairness and equity, I think is sort of a guiding light for us to operate through.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But in terms of the ills of the past, I'm not trying to be cavalier or glib about it.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think it's, you know, we're not sure how to best characterize it.

chapters.summary: Hankerson says if care varies by administration, the city does a disservice to communities. Drury says he cannot speak to past decades and that it is hard to legislate commitment or intent.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks how to ensure equitable park maintenance across administrations

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I mean, I would take from your answer that, you know, the responsibility of caring for facilities differs from administration to administration based off the answer that you just gave.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If that's the case, then we're doing a disservice to the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So how do we ensure that that doesn't happen, no matter who the mayor is, no matter who the parks commissioner is, no matter who the city council is?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: How do we ensure that doesn't happen so that communities, whether they be communities of color or any other community, low-income communities, don't face these challenges decade after decade, and then we are forced to deal with a systemic issue that keeps growing and growing and growing?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a great question and a challenging one to answer.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: You know, I think it's one of the challenges of...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: City government or government at all is that, you know, when you have administrations that have term limits

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: and, you know, there are policy changes, I'm happy having been here, having been through a few different administrations, I'm just, at least in terms I can speak to the last couple administrations, I've experienced, I think, a fairly strong commitment to equity in the parks realm.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But I can't really speak to, you know, the years and decades, and, you know, and none of us are fortune tellers.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It is, I hear you loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I don't know, though, I don't know that there is a way to

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: legislate commitment, if there is a way to legislate intent, if there is a way to, you know, and I think I hear you loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think that's

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's a challenging notion.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'm not really sure how to address.

chapters.summary: Bornstein says the financial obligation to maintain all public assets in good repair is a problem no city has solved. He describes the AIMS program and says the city is behind on preventative maintenance and capital funding.
chapters.title: Bornstein says citywide capital maintenance backlog is massive

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I think my colleague's answer is right, that it's a large issue that transcends the Parks Department, certainly, and transcends any one administration, certainly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I mean, citywide, you know, all of the publicly owned assets, libraries, police stations, et cetera, parks resources, parks facilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The financial obligation to maintain them in a state of good repair is something I know of no city that has solved as a financial question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Setting aside the question of equity, setting aside simply how you prioritize, simply the cost and the ongoing cost of maintaining all public assets in a state of good repair.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I would venture to say, I wager, most cities, if not all cities, have failed to solve that problem, and ours is no exception.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We do many things to assess the value and the condition of our assets.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The city has its AIMS program run by OMB, Asset Inventory Management System, that requires on a four-year basis, I believe, a team to assess the physical condition of every publicly owned asset.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: This is typically buildings, bridges.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Retaining walls and the like, and identify deficiencies that are observable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Again, this is a fairly high level flyby.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Maybe they'll do four buildings in a day, so it's not the deep dive you would get if you focused on a particular asset.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But they will assess the condition of a physical asset, note the deficiencies, and it's part of the city's annual financial calculation in terms of its bonding capacity and its charter obligations.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So we identify that sort of deficiency, what the cost to bring the capital assets into a state of good repair might be.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But OMB, the city, the government, the administration, any administration's ability to actually meet that funding gap, it's beyond my ability to describe how one might get there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But I would venture to say that we're behind in that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And that affects the park's portfolio as well as it affects every other agency's portfolio of capital assets.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We're behind in our ability to fund.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Preventive maintenance, regular annual maintenance, the stuff that we all do for our homes to make sure the roof doesn't leak or the boiler doesn't fail.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The city's behind.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And when you get to a 100-year-old facility, heavily used, multiple facilities of such condition,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The costs are exorbitant.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The costs are staggering.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So if we could fund a capital project to bring a asset into a state of good repair, update its mechanical systems, bring it into compliance with the ADA, bring it into compliance with the city's energy code, it's a major multiple year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Tens if not hundreds of millions of dollar investment, that's one project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Then there's the next one, then there's the next one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So the scale of the problem is simply massive.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And any program that would put in place a strategic plan to get there is a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: You need good data.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: You need to create decent cost estimates on detailed knowledge of existing conditions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Then a whole question about prioritization.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Is it the worst first or the most used first or disadvantaged neighborhoods first?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Those are all valid approaches, and they're probably all correct.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Then you're into a competition for this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The available resource that can be brought into play to address the challenge.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So we love this question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I guess you've already guessed I could talk about this all day, but the solutions are challenging.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Hankerson returns to the rec center evaluations and asks what they found. Bornstein says most capital assets are in relatively poor repair and that Parks ranks asset classes by condition to advocate for capital funding.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks what rec center evaluations found and how assets are ranked

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But just to kind of reset and go back to the initial question is, what did those evaluations find?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The evaluations found that most of our capital assets are in a relatively poor state of good repair.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We have surveyed, I believe, if not all, most of the rec centers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We're trying to survey all of the public restroom buildings.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Our retaining wall portfolio, even things like synthetic turf fields to make sure we understand the condition.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's a relatively new program, 10 years, new-ish.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's a small program.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But with this program in place and the data they're generating,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We can do high-level cost estimating.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We can't do invasive testing or probes or environmental testing to determine the presence of contaminants and such.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: This program can't do that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's run by internal staff.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Parks staffers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But we can and have developed a comprehensive view of each asset class's status so we can rank them in terms of state of good repair.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We can identify critical deficiencies and we can then advocate that those should be

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: funded as capital projects and have begun to do so.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So that was my next question.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It was, is there a ranking?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Since you said there is a ranking, can you tell me by which neighborhoods those rankings, specifically with the recreation centers?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Yeah, it's not.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I mean, I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'd be happy to share it with you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'd be happy to present it to the council if that were an opportunity that you'd be interested in.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'd probably get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But it's not.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You can never get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: By condition.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The rankings are by condition.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So each asset is scored on its delta from what a state of good repair might look like, how far away is it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And obviously newer buildings, recently built buildings that have only been in operation a few numbers of years, they're in great shape and they could be maintained in a great shape indefinitely if that investment in preventive

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: annual maintenance were made.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The older buildings, my colleague mentioned WBA portfolio, some of them are 100 years old, adapted from prior uses, buildings of beautiful buildings,

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Hamfish Recreational Center, the Red Hook Rec Center, all these buildings that have been around forever.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: They're in bad shape and they rank highly in terms of their state of

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: good repair deficit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: They rank highly in terms of the Parks Department's priorities in order to advocate for funding to provide a capital project to renovate them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Many of those have been funded.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Some we can do what's called a CPSD, a capital project, scope development project through OMB to get a detailed cost estimate and forensic testing so we can be very, very specific in the deficiencies and the cost required to address them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And those then enter into sort of a competition for the next round of capital funding for capital investment by the Parks Department.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And, you know, it's a program that we're actually quite happy of, that we can anticipate the next need and the need next to that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It becomes, again, allocation of finite resources.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Will they get funded?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Will they get funded this year?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Are there staff available to work on them?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: You know, allocation of resources becomes the challenge there.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

chapters.summary: Hankerson cites studies that lack of recreation space affects community well-being and asks if that is considered. Bornstein says new rec centers like Shirley Chisholm were placed in neighborhoods historically lacking such facilities.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks if lack of recreation space affects prioritization

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You know, there are studies that show.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: That the lack of recreation spaces have a direct impact on a community's well-being.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Given that, do we take that into consideration when prioritizing what locations need to be addressed or invested into?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yes, I'm speaking, I was speaking about the existing buildings and again, whether they are in a state of good repair or not.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: In addition to that, and again, Shirley Chisholm is the first of six new rec centers that were funded in prior administrations that are now

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Coming online, Shirley Chisholm in Brooklyn was the first to open, and it served a neighborhood that historically had never had any facility of its type.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: This is a state-of-the-art, very, very sophisticated, very, very robustly programmed building that provides all kinds of recreational, educational opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: As you know, I hope you visited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Swimming pool, gymnasium, basketball, classroom, a teaching kitchen, on and on and on.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's an incredible facility.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And at the ribbon cutting, many elected officials spoke about how the conversation about placing that rec center

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: in that neighborhood went back decades, starting from violence on the street, young New Yorkers who were subject to violence, having no safe haven, no place to go.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And the rec center was seen as a solution to those social problems.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We couldn't be stronger advocates for that approach.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But as I said, going back two, three administrations, six projects were funded.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Mary Callie Dalton in Staten Island was the next one to come online.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We started work on Brownsville.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We started work in other neighborhoods in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's a whole list.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I don't want to bore you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But each of those was identified as a location to build a new rec center where none had been previously, or one had been there, but it was in a terrible state of good repair, replace and upgrade.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: In no small part because of the recognition of the value that those facilities provide to their communities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: well above and beyond simply, you know, a place to swim.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I mean, no disrespect by cutting you off.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Not at all, please.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I want to get to my colleagues, but you lead me into my next question.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks about the five new fully accessible recreation centers cited in the transition plan. Bornstein lists Shirley Chisholm, Mary Kelly Dalton, Walter Gladwin, Roy Wilkins, Brownsville, and Soundview, with Brownsville scheduled for 2030.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks where new rec centers will be built and when they open

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The transition plan cites an estimated $500 million investment in five new fully accessible recreation centers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Obviously, Shirley Chisholm is one of those centers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Where will the others be built?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: When will they open?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And will they offer adaptive programming from day one?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And how are those locations selected?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Can answer most of those questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: How they were selected, I wasn't part of that process.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I can't speak personally.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Perhaps you can.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, I can provide a little.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I wasn't directly involved, but our planning division worked closely with our public programs and recreation division, which will be operating these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I think as Commissioner Borsten sort of referenced, there was an assessment about where the gaps, where each of these new facilities, which is to say for the ones that aren't replacement of existing facilities, we found, we identified.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Very striking gaps in which recreation facilities were sorely lacking.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Doesn't mean that there aren't still gaps, of course, and I think that remains, you know, like an ongoing project where we always want to identify new locations.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But for this sort of tranche, if you will, of new centers, there was definitely demographic and geographic analysis done to make sure that we're delivering these facilities where they're most needed.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But to the specific locations themselves.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And before I recite the list, and again, it's a very impressive list.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It represents a scale of investment that none of us can recall, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Six new rec centers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: centers being designed and built all more or less contemporaneously.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Prior to that, we opened the Ocean Breeze Athletic Center in Staten Island in like 2010.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Prior to that, nobody could remember the last time we built a new rec center.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So I think it was the Chelsea Center in like the 90s or something.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So this level of investment was really unprecedented in recent time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: No surprise, I'm sure, if I say I'd love to see it continue sort of on a consistent basis.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: There's a long way to go.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And even after these six buildings open, there will still be parts of this city that don't have convenient or ready access to similar facilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: They live in sort of parks gaps or recreation gaps.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And those resources are another sign of the work that needs to be done, not just to keep the facilities we have operational and in a good state of repair, a state of good repair, but to address the inequity for where those facilities simply don't exist.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So Shirley Chisholm, we know, opened in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Construction has started on, construction is nearing completion on Mary Kelly Dalton in Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: That's the replacement of a facility that was destroyed by Superstorm Sandy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We broke ground recently on Walter Gladwin in the Bronx, and we will be breaking ground, I believe, relatively recently.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It may have already happened.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I may have missed it on the Roy Wilkins Rec Center in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We're working with DDC on these six buildings.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: DDC is actively engaged in the procurement of

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: of a design-build partner for the Brownsville Recreation Center in Brooklyn, and they have completed design on the Soundview Recreation Center in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So all six moving forward, either well on their way to completion or getting started with construction on site, Brownsville being the last of them to be completed, scheduled for completion in 2030.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Using the design-build method that the DDC has pioneered to accelerate project delivery on capital projects of this scale.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks how many pools have working lifts or sloped entries and what inspections showed. Drury says all Olympic and intermediate pools have operational lifts, and all eight beaches have mobility mats and beach wheelchairs.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about pool lifts, working lifts, and beach mobility mats

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to speed through my final three questions.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If you can just keep your answers limited, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Unlikely, sir, but I'll try.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Parks has thoroughly inspected only 11 of its 48 pools, and 36 have some accessible features.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Of those 36, how many have a working lift or sloped entry, and what did the 11 inspections show?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yes, so just to clarify, there are, as I recall, this is a reference to that part of the, that is a reference to our outdoor pools.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There's 53, which include 14 Olympic, 22 intermediate, and 17 pools.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: 41 of them have lifts.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: All of the Olympic and intermediate pool have lifts, and they're all operational.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Or they were this, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: They were fully operational throughout the summer.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Five out of our 17 mini pools have lifts.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: As you may be familiar, our mini pools are relatively

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: small in size, and that is actually just a size capacity issue.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Nine of the 14 Olympic pools have ramps, kind of leading, like sort of built into the pool basin, if you will.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: One of our mini pools has a ramp.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So broadly speaking, you know,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that a variety of our outdoor pools, the majority of our outdoor pools, have accessibility measures of this sort, and they're kept in good condition.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What percentage of pool lifts were working on opening day this past season?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are lifeguards trained to operate them?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: 100% of them were operational throughout the beach and pool season in the outdoor pool portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Lifeguards are not trained to use the pool lifts as their primary focus is on keeping pool patrons safe, largely in the water.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: However, all M&O staff that are on site at a given pool are fully trained to operate the pool lifts, and it is not uncommon.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: M&O staff are also trained to show patrons, if they prefer, how to operate the lifts themselves.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So there's a range to make sure that all of our pool visitors can enjoy the lifts.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are they located at all of the pool sites?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yes, they're on site routinely, correct.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: How many beaches have mobility mats and beach wheelchairs available, and how does the public find out where they are?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, great question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Beaches are a real access challenge, obviously, but we work hard to make sure that visitors of all abilities can come out and enjoy that sand, right, and that sea.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: All eight of our beaches have mobility mats, often multiple locations.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The exact locations of these mats are available on our accessible beaches page on our agency website.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Additionally, the agency also provides beach wheelchairs to beachgoers at no cost.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And a new change that we're very excited about is there's now an online reservation system so that folks can reserve equipment in advance.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'd like to pass it to my colleague, Councilmember Marano, for his questions.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how much it costs to replace a conventional swing with an accessible swing and whether it requires a capital project. Drury says it does not always require a capital project but can be complicated by footings, clearances, and site conditions.
chapters.title: Morano questions Parks on cost and logistics of accessible swings

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate the testimony and the good work that Parks employees do, particularly in my borough, which is the borough of Parks, as you know.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You indicated in your testimony that approximately 900 playgrounds have swing sets and nearly half already have other accessible swings.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yet you're expressing some logistical and operational concerns about legislation that gives you until 2036.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I want to ask a very basic question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, it's a multifaceted question, although basic.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How much does it cost to replace a conventional swing set with an accessible swing where the existing equipment and site conditions permit it?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And does that necessarily require a capital project?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does it require an architect?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does it require this lengthy procurement process?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because I do have a hard time explaining to a parent why something as fundamental as their child being able to enjoy a swing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Could take another decade.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A child who's five years old today could be getting their driver's license by the time we finish installing playground swings.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What are we doing here?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And there's no doubt that accessible swings are remarkably popular.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's why they're basically a standard any time a playground with a swing set is being renovated.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's absolutely like sort of a standard expectation.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: for us.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That reference in the testimony is actually really more germane to the fact that the bill as it's currently drafted would require the installation of accessible swings at all playgrounds, full stop.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Not the way the bill's currently drafted, it doesn't actually, it's irrespective of whether there is a swing set or not.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So that's our largest practical consideration with the bill as it's currently drafted.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But in principle, we hear loud and clear that any park, playground, excuse me, with a swing set,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: whenever possible should have accessible swings for sure.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Your question is, does it always require a capital project?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There are, we do have a finite capacity to swap, if you will, or replace swings equipments.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I will note that it is not as simple as one might think or hope.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It does require significant, you know, the footings, if you will, are not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Broadly speaking, an accessible swing actually, you know, will not necessarily leave enough room or clearance for the adjacent swing.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Like there are, it is a little more complicated than one might think, but there are other avenues to get that work done.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano says Parks' published ADA complaint procedure gives people 60 days after becoming aware of a violation to file. He asks whether Parks would revisit the policy so complaints can be filed as long as a barrier exists, and Titus says Parks probably should.
chapters.title: Morano challenges Parks' 60-day ADA complaint filing window

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I found something in the committee briefing that the staff prepared that I found a little unbelievable, and I'm hoping you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Under Parks'published ADA complaint procedure, a person with a disability has 60 days after becoming aware of a violation to file a complaint.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Parks has identified accessibility problems dating back to the blue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Bloomberg administration and its transition plan doesn't establish an overall completion date.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If someone discovers an inaccessible entrance, waits 61 days, and discovers that it's still inaccessible, will Parks entertain that complaint?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How is it that the person in the wheelchair is on the clock but the government isn't?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm wondering if we can maybe do something as simple as just commit to revisiting that policy so that complaints about ongoing accessibility barriers can be filed for as long as the barrier exists.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate the question.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: I'll just say this, that typically when we receive complaints, usually they're sort of like in real time, and I understand what you're getting at, sort of post-

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: 60 days will we look at that complaint?

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And I think considering that we feel like accessibility is a concern or something that is important to us, I think we would and we probably should revisit the policy.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether a parent in a wheelchair can reach a child, open gates, and access bathrooms in playgrounds. Bornstein says renovated playgrounds are designed to be fully accessible for all visitors, including accessible routes, gates, and seating.
chapters.title: Morano asks whether playgrounds are designed for parents with disabilities

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm the father of two young children, so I spend a fair amount of time thinking about playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And we've talked a lot today about making playgrounds accessible to children with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd also like to ask about parents with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If a father in a wheelchair takes his able-bodied four-year-old to a playground and that child falls and hurts himself, can the father actually get to his child?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can he open the playground gate?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can he reach?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: the play areas?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can he take his child to the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does Parks specifically evaluate playground designs from the perspective of a parent with a disability rather than just a child with a disability?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We certainly do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So again, not speaking to the older, unimproved parks that could be in a variety of conditions with a variety of obstacles that may or may not be there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: In a renovated park, reconstructed playground, the playground is designed to be fully accessible for everybody.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Again, you know, our R&D coordinator, Eddie, is here who can speak at length.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'm not aware of provisions within the design standard that speak to accessible dimensions for children, but for all visitors to the park.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So in a playground, the equipment is designed to be accessible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: There are benches where a wheelchair-bound adult could sit and a companion seat available for them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: All the dimensions for accessible routes through the playground itself between each section of play equipment is accessible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The gate is designed to be operable by somebody with disabilities, again, in full compliance with the design standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And even the safety surface material, which is a thick rubberized mat designed for safety, the transition from grade, which might be asphalt, up onto that mat of safety surface equipment, even that transition is designed to be in compliance

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: for any adult or any person visiting the park who might have a disability.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether a 30-year-old active duty Marine would pay $150 while a veteran pays $25. Drury confirms the current distinction and says Parks is still assessing the fiscal impact of Intro 1177.
chapters.title: Morano asks why active duty military pay more than veterans for rec centers

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If I can ask one last question, it'll spare everybody a second round.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As chair of the Veterans Committee and a sponsor of Intro 1177, I was very pleased to hear your favorable comments about the intent of our legislation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I do want to ask something.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Under your current fee structure, could a 30-year-old active duty Marine be charged $150 for a recreation center membership while a 30-year-old veteran would pay?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If so, what's the rationale behind that distinction?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Has the agency calculated how much revenue would actually forgo by extending the discount to active duty military personnel?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Excellent question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And the short answer is the scenario you provided.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The active duty individual would not be eligible for that discount.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Although if they have an ID NYC card, they get a 10% discount.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But leaving that aside, whereas the veteran would.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And we hear, I think we've heard loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The short answer is that this bill is fairly, was just introduced.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We are actually still assessing potential fiscal impacts, you know, are inclined to hope that they would be relatively minimal in the grand scheme of things.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But this feels like, you know, just ideologically a fair and logical discussion to have.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether the ADA coordinator is full-time and who is responsible for correcting violations. Bornstein says the role is full-time but focused on active or planned capital projects, not citywide surveys or 311 complaints.
chapters.title: Hanif asks if ADA coordinator is full-time and who ensures corrections

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you for your great questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
