utterances.text: And Commissioner Borsten, I appreciate your honesty about what you've shared about the state of disrepair of much of our

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: our parks infrastructure, which is why I think it makes the role of the ADA coordinator even more urgent and critical.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And could you confirm if the ADA coordinator is a full-time position?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And when the ADA coordinator identifies an accessibility violation, who is responsible for ensuring it's corrected?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So again, our at Capital ADA coordinator's role is on active or planned capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So not in general, not surveying the whole city, not responding to 311 complaints or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But when we...

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Begin looking at a site for a capital project or begin working on that project, any existing deficiencies, whether

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: the coordinator himself identifies them or others, become part of the project scope for that project conditions that the new design will be required or intended to address.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The coordinator's role there is to make sure that as the design evolves, those issues are met, as is full compliance with the design standard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And as we enter into construction and things get tough in the field with site conditions and unknown conditions and gradients and whatnot, part of his responsibility is to help everyone on site mitigate any concerns that arise.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So if...

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We start a project with a known set of ADA non-compliances.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The team, of which Eddie is a member, will make sure those issues are addressed as part of the delivery of that project.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether the ADA coordinator must sign off before capital projects are approved or opened. Bornstein says he is not aware of an accessibility sign-off, though the coordinator can direct redesigns when issues arise.
chapters.title: Bornstein says ADA coordinator does not sign off on capital projects

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so is the coordinator then required to sign?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: sign off on capital project before they are approved or open to the public?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And it is right behind me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I can ask him, but his role.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: He's smiling.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: He's probably laughing at me, struggling to answer a question he could answer right off the top of his head.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So, you know, sign offs are interesting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The Department of Building signs off on our site.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We have a role called special inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: They sign off on our sites.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Make sure everything is designed in accordance with the designs and specs, the drawings and specs for that project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Of course, building code compliance, safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Eddie, is there an accessibility sign-off that anybody provides?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'm not aware of one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: No, okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then can the ADA coordinator require...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The department to make accessibility improvements?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Yes, but you shouldn't have to.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Because the coordinator role is advising on the design phase and the design standards as opposed to existing facilities and surveying them.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Who's surveying existing facilities?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: For accessibility issues.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: A team from Capital would go out and assess the site.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It could be a part of that team.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Likewise, consult.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And what is that team?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is that team called something?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So as we're scoping a project, we develop scopes and cost estimates in practice with council members.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So you know this process of identifying a need.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We work with council members of their priorities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We identify what projects are of most importance to you and your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Then we go out and do an assessment of the condition of that site and the probable cost that we develop a budget in consideration of funding.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Those assessments are made by the capital design staff, landscape architects, predominantly civil engineers who will go out and look at gradients.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Architects will go out and look at architectural features like public restroom buildings and note deficiencies there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: All those observations become scopes of work, tracked to cost estimates.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: They become scope for a capital project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And if Eddie were to look at us or really anyone, but Eddie most notably, as those designs evolve, if he were to say, you know what, that right there wasn't designed properly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He is authorized to direct the team to do a redesign and address that deficiency.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: That's, you know, again, not the only one, because, again, as I said earlier, the landscape architects who design these things and their supervisors are similarly trained to know how to design in compliance with the design standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It is oversight is invaluable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He will note things that others might miss because it's his specific area of expertise.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many parks spaces the ADA coordinator currently advises. Bornstein says the capital portfolio has over 500 active jobs and Eddie gets involved in projects that rise to his attention through an escalating review process.
chapters.title: Bornstein says ADA coordinator advises projects that rise to his attention

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So how many?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Parks, spaces are currently being advised by the ADA coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Well, we have an active portfolio of over 500 jobs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's not, I'm not here to say that Eddie is involved in all of them, but through sort of an escalating series of conversations, Eddie gets involved in the ones that rise to his level of attention.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So he reports to the chief of design for landscape at Capitol.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: That chief is responsible for making sure all designs are done in compliance with our design standard and all codes and laws.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And Eddie advises him as part of his team will review projects at various stages of development of design and comment on them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So, again, it's a big portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Once Eddie has reviewed something and basically given it his approval, it moves on into construction.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: He'll revisit the site in construction and make sure that nothing has arisen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Mostly he will respond to calls.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I think we have a dimensional problem.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Can you come out and take a look?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Or I think we're going to have a problem.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Can you come out and take a look?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And again, this happens proactively too as we're anticipating starting a job to go out and make sure we understand what needs to be done to bring a site into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And again, if we're replacing all of, let's say, 50-year-old playground equipment, the design standards have changed industry-wide.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So an industry exists today that never existed 50, I would say 40 or 30 years ago

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: of manufacturers of playground equipment that know how to build, know how to design compliant equipment that meets the needs of all levels of age.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: You know, children of different ages, but also all level of disability.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So it's not one size fits all.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: It's not there is a ADA park and a non-ADA park.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: There are many choices that we make as we're identifying which types of equipment we want to bring in.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Not all parks have swings.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So not all playgrounds have swings.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So those choices get made to try to address what we've heard from the community members who participate in our community engagement process, which is an ongoing dialogue throughout design.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And of course, at various milestones, we present back to community boards and their parks committees and ultimately to the Public Design Commission.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And if we took a wrong turn somewhere or missed something important, many opportunities to call our attention to that, we'll make a course correction and fix it.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many ADA-related complaints Parks received in recent fiscal years. Rain Credo says the office received about 50 accommodation requests or complaints in 2026 to date, 27 in 2025, and 49 in 2024.
chapters.title: Rain Credo reports 50 accommodation requests in 2026, 27 in 2025, 49 in 2024

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so how many ADA-related complaints has Parks received in the last fiscal year?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And are you able to provide us with complaints received?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: over the last three fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Sure, so this is in the context, traditionally, and if I misterm this, Rain and others will correct me, but in the realms of what we would kind of like reasonable accommodation requests, and I think that's a context in which Commissioner Titus and Rain can provide, I think the last few

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: fiscal years or calendar years, one or the other, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: So in 2026 to date, we have received a total of like 50 accommodation requests slash complaints.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: They are all kind of grouped together.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: It can be a little challenging to separate out like a complaint versus an accommodation request.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: In 2025, we received a total of 27.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: In 2024, we received a total of 49 RA requests.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And what's the status of the reasonable accommodations?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And you said that there might be some other issues.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you maybe provide...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Some more context as to what's been resolved and what's pending?

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Yeah, so there are some complaints that are easily resolvable, like pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Something like we can get a complaint about a MobiMat that has too much sand on it.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Removing that sand is a pretty easy, straightforward request that we can quickly fulfill.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: And then

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Other times we'll get complaints about the structure of a facility.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: And a complaint like that would clearly take much more time to address.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: So the status of the request, the time that it takes to address it can take.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Time depending on what it is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So are you keeping track of the reasonable accommodation requests that came in over this last year, what the status is of whether or not those accommodations have been approved or denied?

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: For, again, for, like, the larger requests, those are pending still because they take more time.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: That is to say that, like, we respond to these patrons and we let them know that, like, thank you for calling in for this request and that it will take time to address.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: But, again, like, the...

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Other ones that are faster to address, we very quickly reach out and let them know what has been decided.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Can you share with this committee what kinds of reasonable accommodation requests have come in?

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: We get reasonable accommodation requests for people to bring their service animals to our pools.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: We get accommodation requests for our gardens, specific gardens, to be made more accommodative for people.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: We get requests for people to people.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: to bring their medical devices to swim areas as well.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: And that would be just like a handful of the types of requests that we get.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what kinds of reasonable accommodation requests Parks receives and which take longest. Credo cites service animals, medical devices, garden access, and chairlift requests, saying structural requests take much longer.
chapters.title: Rain Credo describes reasonable accommodation requests and chairlift delays

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And what are the kinds of reasonable accommodations that take the longest to get approved?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm assuming medical devices, service animals,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are those not quick?

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Those are pretty quick.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Yes, so for a request that would take a while,

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Oh, this is such a great question.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: I guess one that comes to mind would be the request to put in a chairlift, for example.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: That is something that, like...

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: We would need to assess the area to be sure that we can actually put something like that in, what the cost of it would be, how long it would take to install it, and then maintaining it.

utterances.speaker: Rain Credo
utterances.text: Something like that would take more time.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's a good example.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How costly is installing a chairlift, and how many of our facilities that should have chairlifts are in compliance?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, in terms of the average cost of a chairlift, I think, and there are obviously different configurations.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Most of our, as we testified already, the majority of our pools have them.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There are other scenarios in which they're inside of buildings.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of their average cost, I think we need to look closer into that, except that it is often provided as a...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Accessibility solution as part of a larger capital project.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's often the case.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But in terms of an actual average cost, I think it's hard to segment out that element.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, we'll circle back about the cost.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to pass it to Council Member Joseph for her questions.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks what feedback MOPD gave on Parks' Local Law 12 accessibility plan and how many complaints MOPD received about Parks. Meherig says the feedback predates her time and she will share information with the committee.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about MOPD feedback on Parks' five-year accessibility plan

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I have a question around Local Law 12 that requires agencies to write the accessibility plans in consultation with MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What feedback did MOPD give on Parks Plan, and was it adopted?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many complaints about Parks did MOPD receive last year?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We were proud to work alongside MOPD in complying with Local Law 12.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It is available.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The report is available on our website, and I believe there's even been a progress report or two that have been posted since to help characterize MOPDs, and as I understand it, a multi-agency effort to characterize and give a little color about that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'll ask the Deputy Commissioner to chime in a bit.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Balkeis Meherig
utterances.text: The feedback on the five-year accessibility plan was before my time, so I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You can share it with the committee.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many accessible park restrooms stay open year-round and how quickly snow and ice are cleared. Drury says most of about 700 restroom buildings stay open year-round and snow clearance prioritizes perimeters and sidewalks.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about year-round restrooms and snow clearance on accessible routes

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Winter access.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The hearing comes to right before winter.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many accessible park restrooms stay open year-round?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How quickly does park clear snow and ice from accessible routes, ramps, and entrances?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thanks for that question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We have roughly 700 or so park restroom buildings in our public restroom buildings in our portfolio, the vast majority of which are kept open year round.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There are a few located near our beaches, what have you, that have to be winterized essentially to avoid bursting pipes, what have you.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So by and large, they are kept open year round, broadly speaking.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of snow clearance, depending on the severity of the snow, but we have a well-established standard operating procedure through which park perimeters, especially any bus stations, fire hydrants, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: are cleared, that's the very top priority.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And then we kind of work in from there, addressing park interiors and other sort of common areas as availability, as we can kind of work into that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But generally speaking, we prioritize perimeters and sidewalks first so people can get where they're going.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That window is what, 24 hours, 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You said depend on the snow.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It can vary entirely.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, as we've seen with some super severe snows, that can be a real, a very serious undertaking.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But we do everything in our power to make sure it's cleared as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many recreation centers and major parks have accessible drop-off spots for Access-A-Ride. Drury says Parks cannot characterize that today but says proximity to public transportation is a core factor for new facilities.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about Access-A-Ride drop-offs and transit routes to parks

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The ADA requires accessible routes from transit stops and parking to park features.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many recreation centers and major parks have an accessible drop-off spot for Access-A-Ride?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Does the park work with DOT and MTA on routes from the nearest accessible subway station?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that a conversation you have interagency?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think I would twofold.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I don't think we can characterize today how many of our existing recreation centers have a drop-off location in the way that you described it.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think we'd have to circle back on that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But I will say that when it comes– and these opportunities don't come along very often, but I can say that when choosing the location for a new facility, proximity to public transportation is a very core component of that decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks what rules require Parks to keep accessible routes open or post alternatives during construction. Bornstein says Rupert Park will close entirely during construction and then reopen with fully accessible routes, except one quadrant for a restroom building.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how Parks maintains accessible routes during Rupert Park construction

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I have another one real quick for you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In the Rupert Park reconstruction will run its phase until 2029.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When the capital project closes, closes paths or entrance, what rule require parks to keep accessible routes open or post alternative routes?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Who checks on that?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When you need to have alternative routes opening during a construction, that may not take up all of the park.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Oh, in terms of how the construction is being phased.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That project happens to be a phased project.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Glad to try to answer your question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: I'm delighted that you're familiar with Rupert Park.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: We're very proud of it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: As you may know, the existing site is steeply sloped, and the park exists before we began construction as a series of sort of isolated...

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Plazas with staircases separating them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So accessibility was really almost non-existent.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The new design will be fully accessible and all parts of the park will be accessible, compliant with the design standard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And those won't be ramps.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Those will be those shallow sloped grades.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: The public restroom building in the southeast corner of the park is being developed as a second project for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So the contractor will close the entire park.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: That's already happened.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: Begin to do demolition and regrading the entire park.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And then they will begin to reconstruct the park so that the three quarters of the park to the north and the west and whatever, other than the PRB portion, will all open at once.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And all the pathways within the park will be accessible routes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: They'll be all accessible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: There are multiple entrances that will be reopened at that point.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: All the playground equipment, really everything.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: and the dog run all be accessible to the public and fully accessible from a accessibility point of view, except for that one quadrant to the south, which is going to be closed to the public to facilitate the construction of the public restaurant building.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And that'll open, of course, you know, subsequently that at that point, the entire park will be accessible.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm happy the park girls will like that.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether Parks offers sensory-friendly hours or trains staff to support visitors with autism. Drury says Parks incorporates sensory aspects into capital projects and offers adaptive programming, and Titus describes disability etiquette training.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about sensory-friendly hours and autism training

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Chair, can I have two more, please, real quick?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When we talked about sensory and cognitive disabilities, when we talk about beyond sensory gardens and playgrounds, does the park offer sensory-friendly hours at recreation centers or events,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: or front-line staff trained to support visitors with autism or intellectual disabilities?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, thanks for that question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We definitely pride ourselves on, you know, not only the physical facilities, playgrounds, what have you, you know, and Commissioner Borsten, obviously, you know, the fact that we incorporate sort of sensory aspects into all of our capital projects, we're very proud of that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of programming, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: You know, our recreation centers are, you know, we...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: People of all abilities, children of all abilities, our summer camp programs, you know, our employees are well trained and sensitive to those alternative needs.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think we're proud to offer a range of adaptive programming, you know, in a variety of different fashions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And your summer program is an amazing program.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It's one of the best kept secrets in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks who is responsible for ADA compliance at playgrounds shared with schools. Drury says those are jointly operated playgrounds under public school jurisdiction but managed day to day by Parks, which typically advances capital improvements.
chapters.title: Joseph asks who handles ADA compliance at jointly operated playgrounds

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So schools who share playgrounds with some playgrounds next to schools are run by you and the New York.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: New York City public school students use them during the day and the public use them after hours.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Who's responsible for ADA compliance at these sites?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are they covered by parks and transition plan and by the assessment intro 212 would require?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And that's my last question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: No, great question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yes, so those properties that are adjacent to schools, technically New York City public schools jurisdiction, but managed on a day-to-day basis by the Parks Department.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We refer to those as jointly operated playgrounds or JOPs.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of capital improvements that are made, which could include ADA accessibility improvements, obviously, those projects are typically advanced by the Parks Department.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It's usually in very close coordination with the local school, with the NYC public schools writ large.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So I would argue, you know, in terms of advancing the work that's done and making those improvements, Parks generally takes on that responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: For that property.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And then there wasn't, maybe there was, okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: All right, thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Councilmember Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Narcisse praises recreation centers as preventative care and asks whether Parks would site them where children can access them independently. Drury says access to transportation is a prime consideration for new recreation centers.
chapters.title: Narcisse supports rec centers and asks about transportation access

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You spoke about child abolition, which I love so much.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I was there present.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And like I expressed many ways that we should have more around.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And it will be preventative care for our children, for our youth.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And it will spend less money in anti-gun violence and all that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So let's work together and make it happen for each and every area.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I appreciate the honesty that you came across with, with the testimony, because many areas we know those parks are left.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: to be handled by the community themselves.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Entry 1177, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Sorry to hear what you feel about it, but I feel like we're going to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if you have any, because I co-prime it with council colleagues, showmen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And accessibility, when we talk about accessibility for the parks, right, would you put a rec center in a place where our kids cannot access, or would you put it where there is transportation that can independently get there?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: No, thanks for the question, Councilmember, and we do appreciate the goals and aims of Intro 1177, as you noted.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I will, you know, when it comes time to locate a new or to site a new recreation center, you know, access to transportation is hugely important, and we think it can absolutely, you know, leverage, you know,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: existing infrastructure, you know, and make sure that folks who want to get to that center can get to that center.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think that's something that was definitely a prime consideration for the new centers, the many new centers that are underway.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It would be top priority, I hope, because we need our kids to get to it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You cannot have a center, a hidden center, in a place where the kids cannot get transportation to get there themselves.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks when Parks last did a full accessibility survey and whether the data is public. Drury says Parks assesses its portfolio in many ways but does not have a single unified accessibility survey.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks if Parks has a full accessibility survey and public data

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: When did the Parks Department last do a full accessibility survey of its properties, and is that data public?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So, yeah, thanks.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: For that question, Council Member, and I think this speaks to a little bit of a – the agency assesses its portfolio in a variety of different ways, and that takes many different forms.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's daily inspections.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's our parks inspection program.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That is the sort of state of good repair capital needs assessment team that Commissioner Borsten mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That is also an assessment, a deep assessment of every property that is about to undergo an improvement.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So that, but I don't know that we can say that there is a single unified accessibility survey.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And in fact, I don't know that we'd agree that that would be like an, like.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We believe that the state of our park system is important to assess, but that has multiple components, right?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Like in terms of accessibility, just in terms of its general condition, in terms of energy code, building code, what have you, right?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There are so many different aspects that come into that, and accessibility is a core value for any improvement that we make.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But, you know, so there isn't really a specific accessibility survey that is...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Targeted in quite that limited a manner.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we cannot find a place where we say, okay, this park here, this park there, I cannot go, I'm disabled, I cannot get access, we don't have that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Well, respectfully, accessibility means different things to different people, and what may be accessible for one individual may not be accessible for another.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So it's just another challenge that's, in terms of how people define that accessibility, can be exceedingly challenging.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let's talk about wheelchair or certain things, kids with autism, different things that you can, sensory.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think there are accessibility features that are incorporated into

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: practically all of our major facilities.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Not that they all meet the exacting standards of the 2010 ADA design standards.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's not necessarily the case, but I think by and large, we feel that many of our major facilities offer significant accessibility features.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether recreation center staff, lifeguards, and park enforcement officers are trained to respond to a child with autism in distress. Titus says Parks offers mandated diversity and disability etiquette training that covers intellectual disabilities.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about training for staff responding to children with autism

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let me move forward for that because that's not my hearing, so I can get to my question.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I'm assuming moving forward from 1990, all the capital budget that you undertake will have the full accessibility to build them, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm assuming that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm just saying thank you in advance because everyone can use our report.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Our recreation center staff, lifeguards, and park enforcement, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: patrol officers train on how to recognize and calmly respond to a child with autism who is overwhelmed or in distress.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that a training that require or is just optional for the parks?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And there's a range of employee training that's available.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So I'm going to have Commissioner Titus maybe speak a little more on that.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: So I just wanted to say that we do have like some basic mandated trainings that all of our employees go through every other year.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: It's called our Everybody Matters.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: It's a diversity inclusion training.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: And we do offer diversity disability etiquette training.

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: The exact components to what you just asked, I'm not exactly sure if that's in the training, but I can tell you that the training does cover a lot of different types of disabilities, including intellectual disabilities

utterances.speaker: Ayanna Titus
utterances.text: and how to really interact with patrons who have those challenges.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says Parks can be slow but she loves parks and wants to partner on a recreation center in her district. She thanks the chair and leaves.
chapters.title: Narcisse urges partnership for new rec centers in her district

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You hit the bus, but I'm going to have to leave.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: One of the things that I'm going to say right now, the park department, when it comes to certain things, we're very slow.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But I love parks, no matter what people tell me.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But we have to work together, and especially when it comes to rec center around New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have the opportunity to improve our communities.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I would love to partner and see how we can put one in my district that I'm dying to see because that's where my kids have the most problems.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks Parks to explain its operational capacity concerns with Intro 212. Drury says the bill as drafted seems to mandate a perpetual assessment of every facility on 30,000 acres, while Hanif says ongoing assessment is the point.
chapters.title: Hanif and Drury debate Intro 212's perpetual assessment mandate

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Narcisse, for your questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Just building on the council members'line of questioning around surveying our facilities for accessibility, Intro 212 would get at that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share more?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: about the operational capacity concerns that Parks shared during its testimony.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Sure, thanks for that, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I think what we want to make very clear is that we really want to work collaboratively.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I think there's a...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of our shared goals and in terms of making sure that the public is broadly aware of the accessibility features that are available at a given property.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think there's a lot of work to be done and a lot of improvements to be made in terms of the information that's available.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: In terms of the bill as it's currently drafted, as we are interpreting, as we are reading it thus far, it does seem to mandate the creation of what would essentially be a perpetual, never-ending

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: ongoing assessment of every aspect of every facility of every park property on all 30,000 acres.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I just can't stress strongly enough, like, and maybe that wasn't the intent, and we'd look forward to talking to you more about that, but we can't stress strongly enough that, you know, conceptually,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: It is hard to even get our heads around that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So we'd really like to work with you to figure out, you know, in terms of the true aims and goals.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: If we've misunderstood, you know, we obviously want to work through that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think this is a challenge that every entity that's managing infrastructure faces, whether it's, you know, the MTA or NYCHA, DOT with our street system, right?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The notion of...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: assessing, surveying, you know, the degree to which resources are directed towards that, by definition, would, you know, detract from, you know, efforts to actually make the

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's a very serious concern we have.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: That's not to say that information isn't important.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: As you've heard, there are a variety of different ways in which we're assessing our properties and a variety for a variety of different factors, including accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But we're not sure that the bill as it's currently drafted is the right approach to use our finite resources.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I would certainly push back on that and say that we do need to be a city where every department from parks, MTA, and other public-facing

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: public-facing institutions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Are striving to be fully accessible.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And the perpetual assessment is the point so that we do get to a place where we're able to share that, well, New York City,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: facilities, whether it be the MTA or a playground, were fully accessible and in compliance with the ADA.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So those finite resources, I mean, yes, I think it's a big undertaking at the start, given the state of disrepair that was very honestly

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: shared during today's hearing, but to know that maybe in a couple of years we wouldn't have to hear testimony that is about the disrepair and rather here are the ways in which we are actually

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: including

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: even more modernized pathways for accessible features.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great point, Councilmember, and I think maybe I was, I apologize, a little ungenerous.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think you're hitting on something really important, which is I think to the degree that there's appetite for a broader conversation about how the city treats its infrastructure and how to conceive of it, I think that's something we'd be a glad and willing partner in that conversation for sure.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So apologies if I didn't make that clear earlier.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many of the 49 additional accessibility capital projects have been completed. Bornstein says 47 are completed and two are in active construction.
chapters.title: Parks says 47 of 49 accessibility capital projects completed

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So the 2024-25 accessibility progress reports that 57 capital projects with accessibility improvements were completed as of May 2025 and that parks anticipated completing 49 more.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share how many of those 49 are completed?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No, either one of us could read it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: 47 have been completed, two are in active construction.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Wonderful.

chapters.summary: Hanif notes only one public comment came during the 2024 comment period and asks how Parks advertised it. Drury says he was not directly involved but says Parks typically uses the City Record and email blasts to stakeholders.
chapters.title: Hanif asks how Parks advertised accessibility plan comment period

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Only one public comment came during the March 14th to May 3rd, 2024 comment period.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How did Parks advertise this?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I don't think anyone at this table was involved in the actual execution of said public.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think we'll have to get a better, I suspect, you know, notice in the city record, you know, other conventional messaging opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I'm getting, you know, perhaps, you know, emails to community boards.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I wasn't directly involved, but we can get a little more clarity on how that comment period was publicized.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: How are the comment periods usually publicized?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is there a standard process or is it project by project?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think it depends on the mechanics of the fact of the matter is we don't engage in so many exercises that require a formal comment period.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So it's hard to characterize broadly speaking.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But I know that the city record is a sort of standard that's available, publicly available, obviously, to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And then typically for, let's call it procedural announcements, it's not uncommon for us to try to utilize.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Email blasts to elected officials, community boards, other key stakeholders of that nature.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I know that, for example, that's what we do through the City Administrative Procedural Act, CAPA rule changes.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There's sort of a formal, now that's a little more formally, the details of that a little more formally set out in the administrative code, so that's maybe not the best example, but there are a variety of ways in which we try to make

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: comment periods open through our website or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Understood.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks which facility classes have full inventories and when the rest will. Drury says Parks has largely completed recreation centers and is midstream on public restrooms and retaining walls, and will circle back with a status update.
chapters.title: Hanif asks which facility classes have full accessibility inventories

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The transition plan says full inventories of each facility class will follow the 2020 Historic House Trust Study as a model.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Which facility classes have a full inventory today and when will the rest have one?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, so to clarify, that's a reference to that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: As I understand it, that was sort of a reference to our examination about various particular asset classes.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And the HHT, our historic house portfolio, is fairly finite at 22.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I think the agent, as Commissioner Borsten had noted, we are sort of in the process of working through a variety of other asset classes.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Largely, as I understand, we have largely, if not entirely, made our way through recreation centers.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Public restroom buildings, retaining walls, I think, is still sort of midstream.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: You know, I think we can kind of, it'd probably be easiest to circle, I don't want to misspeak, we should probably circle back and kind of give you a status update on each of those asset classes and the effort.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Wonderful.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what Parks builds when terrain makes 5% walkways impossible. Bornstein explains that 5% slopes avoid ramp requirements, but steeper areas use 1-to-12 ramps and sometimes stairs.
chapters.title: Bornstein explains 5% walkway preference and ramp standards

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then Parks prefers walkways sloped under 5% and avoids stone screenings.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Where terrain makes those standards impossible, what does Parks build instead?

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So the 5% in the accessibility design guidelines is a sloped walkway that is not

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: considered a ramp.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So it doesn't require handrails and the other dimensional features of a ramp.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: A ramp is something steeper at 1 to 12, which is an 8% sort of ramp.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: If we can do something as shallow as 5% or shallower to mitigate grade changes, that's our preference because that's just sort of a natural, sort of easy to navigate pathway that most people wouldn't even really recognize as a grade change.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: If it has to be steeper than that, we'll go to the 1 to 12 and build a limited length of ramp to navigate between two different levels of grade.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: So 1 to 12, you know, one inch per foot for as ever long as it takes to go from one elevation to the next.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: And then limited cases where we can provide staircases as well, we'll provide staircases.

utterances.speaker: Eric Bornstein
utterances.text: But where an accessible route is required, if we can't get away with the one to five, we'll go one to 12 and build a technically build a ramp.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many projects since 2020 needed an exception to accessibility design standards. Drury says Parks is not aware of a formal mechanism to memorialize exceptions and says they are anecdotally uncommon.
chapters.title: Parks says no formal mechanism to track accessibility design exceptions

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then how many projects since 2020 needed an exception to its accessibility design standards?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Yeah, this is so.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: The agency, we're not aware of a formal mechanism, you know, outside of the context of specific reasonable accommodation requests.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: We don't really, there's not really a formal mechanism in place to memorialize an instance in which a proposed accessibility improvement would, you know, would kind of, would require an exception in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think we can.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: can anecdotally tell you it's pretty uncommon.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Our design teams do their best to kind of make sure that it's incorporated wherever feasible.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So I think we can sort of anecdotally characterize that it's pretty uncommon, but we're not aware of a sort of formal written memorialization of that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether Parks believes it already does something like her annual ADA report bill. Drury says the existing Local Law 73 report focuses on recent and upcoming work and is much more limited in scope.
chapters.title: Hanif asks if Parks already reports on ADA compliance

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then just going back to my bill to publish an annual report on Parks'compliance with the ADA, does the department believe it's already doing something like this?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I think we'd say that the, so there is the existing local law, which is, and I'm, you know,

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: I would characterize that the current reporting focuses very much on recent and upcoming work, which we believe is very valuable for the public to know about.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And we think that's important, as we think having readily available information on website or other sources is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So it is similarly themed as Introduction 212, but...

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Fundamentally much more limited in scope.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then does that current manual provide timeline for addressing facilities that aren't meeting the ADA standards?

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So the current reporting is, again, focusing more on recent or active work.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And I believe that for the active works timeline provisions, information is provided, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Hanif says those are all her questions and thanks the administration witnesses. She announces a three-minute break before public testimony.
chapters.title: Hanif closes agency Q&A and announces three-minute break

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Well, those are all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all for your patience.

chapters.summary: The hearing resumes and Hanif opens public testimony. She reminds attendees to observe decorum, explains the three-minute speaking limit, and describes how to submit written testimony.
chapters.title: Hearing resumes and Hanif sets public testimony rules

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: All right, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, would you kindly settle down, find your seats.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We're going to resume the hearing momentarily.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I will now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the sergeant at arms for inclusion at the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: In the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have three minutes to speak on today's oversight topic.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of the testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: For the first panel, I'd like to call Jean Ryan, Monica Bartley, Michael Ring, and Evan Yankee.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
