chapters.summary: Jean Ryan, president of Disabled in Action of Metropolitan New York, says Parks passes the buck on accessibility at zoos, botanical gardens, and the aquarium. She describes inaccessible bathrooms, blocked exhibits, and construction at the Central Park Conservatory Garden.
chapters.title: Jean Ryan testifies on accessibility failures at zoos, gardens, and Central Park

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Hello, I'm Jean Ryan, President of Disabled in Action of Metropolitan New York, DIA for short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: People with disabilities are having problems with policies and facilities in botanical gardens, zoos, and the aquarium, as well as parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And since the city owns the land, parks is ultimately responsible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Typically, when we have an access complaint, if we complain to parks, they say we have to deal with the entity that is running that space, such as WCS or the Brooklyn Botanic Garden or a conservancy like the Central Park Conservancy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: It's a totally inefficient and often unsuccessful way to get access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: There are multiple access problems with the four WCS zoos and the aquarium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We demand that they hire a disability access person who will proactively discover and correct access problems instead of us bringing them up one by one to guest relations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: For years, there has been no truly accessible...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: accessible bathroom at the Central Park Zoo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: At the Bronx Zoo, because of misguided policies, we've been told we cannot get into two exhibits in our motorized wheelchairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: How many people have been turned away to something we pay taxes for and also a hefty entrance fee for?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: There are also bathroom access problems at the Bronx Zoo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: They mean well, but are clueless about accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Projects at Brooklyn Botanic Garden are designed so people with mobility disabilities are left out, such as new areas we cannot access and the pathetic native plant garden that has paths that lead to stairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We cannot get to the Cherry Esplanade, a premier destination for everyone, because of three-inch-high lips that block access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: The city rubber stamps these projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: It's time for the Parks Department to step up and stop passing the buck on accessibility for people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: And then lastly, since I have another minute, I wanted to mention yesterday we wanted to go to the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Conservatory garden in Central Park in the northern part of the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: It's so beautiful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We could see the trees, but we could not get in because there's construction that's going on until 2028.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: People with disabilities, with mobility disabilities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: are blocked from getting in there then until 2028 unless you can do stairs and we can't do stairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: We want to get in that garden and we want to see it and we want to experience it and there's no reason that they can't figure out some way so we can get in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Into it some kind of way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: There's just a big fence and it says, there's a telephone number, call this number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Yeah, what good is that going to do when you're right there trying to get in the garden?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Ryan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Thank you, Jean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: I think that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't get that closer.

chapters.summary: Monica Bartley, a wheelchair user and Disabled in Action member, says inaccessible pathways and facilities prevent her from fully enjoying parks. She describes a restroom door at Central Park's Discovery House that opened inward and blocked her wheelchair, and supports Intro 212's annual assessments and public map.
chapters.title: Monica Bartley describes inaccessible restrooms and supports Intro 212

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: My name is Monica Bartley, a member of Disabled in Action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: I'm a wheelchair user.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Council Member Hanif and other sponsors of this bill for bringing attention to the important issue of accessibility in our city parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Parks are among my happy places.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: They offer opportunities to relax and enjoy nature and spend time with family and friends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: However, as a wheelchair user, I'm often unable to fully enjoy these spaces because of inaccessible pathways and facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Too often, I find myself looking at places I would love to explore but cannot access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Just yesterday, while visiting Central Park with a friend, I attempted to use the restroom at the Discovery House, but could not because the door opened inward, leaving me unable to maneuver my wheelchair

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: and close the door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: We brought this to the attention of the attention of the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: of a parks employee who inspected the restroom and took a picture to report the problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Earlier this year, I also visited Canarsie Park, but was unable to locate an accessible restroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: These experiences demonstrate how accessibility barriers can prevent people with disabilities from fully enjoying our public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: I support this bill's requirements that parks conduct annual assessments of entrances, bathrooms, playgrounds, beaches, and pools to determine ADA compliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Equally important are the requirements for parks to identify necessary improvements, establish timelines for addressing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: barriers, and provide an online map showing the accessibility of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: This information will help people with disabilities plan their visits and know what to expect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: All parks belong to all New Yorkers, including people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Accessibility should not be an afterthought or a matter of chance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Everyone deserves the opportunity to enjoy these public spaces with dignity and independence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: I encourage our council to support these bills and help make our parks truly accessible to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Monica Bartley
utterances.text: and consideration.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Michael Ring, vice president of Disabled in Action of Greater New York, says he plans marathon routes around working drinking fountains and bathrooms. He opposes Intro 212 as an unfunded mandate and says Parks needs more money to fix known accessibility problems.
chapters.title: Michael Ring says Parks knows problems but lacks funding, opposes unfunded mandate

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Michael Ring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I'm vice president of Disabled in Action of Greater New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: And if anyone needs a verbal description of my appearance, I'm a 63-year-old white guy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I need a shave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: My hair's a mess.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I wear a pair of ankle braces when I leave the house.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I'm wearing a hoodie that says I ran the London Marathon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I ran five marathons this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I'm running my sixth in two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I'm not bragging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Well, yeah, I am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: But I trained for all these marathons in New York City parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: All different parks in every borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I plan my routes around where drinking fountains are going to be and where bathrooms are going to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Accessibility means different things to a lot of different people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: A water fountain that you got to, that you can't, that the button doesn't work is not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But it doesn't work for anybody, really, if only water comes out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And I fill out 311 complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I call the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And they say they know about it, but they don't have any money to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So that's why I'm not really in support of Intro 20212, because the parks, and I talk to the park people, they know what the problems are about accessibility, about everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: They just don't have any money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And this bill seems like an unfunded mandate, that they're going to be asked to hire new people, people who are experts in accessibility to go into bathrooms and look at things with tape measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: These are known problems, and the Parks Department needs a lot more money to fix them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: They get a teeny percent of the city's budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And it got me thinking about similar events that the city has that are like parks but are not parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I really enjoyed the Summer Streets events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: In chunks, I ran all the way from Chambers Street to Dyckman, you know, all the way up Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That's about 200 blocks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And each block had...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: At least five police officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That's four, that's a thousand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: police officers on overtime all day, three times for these three events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I was just imagining how much this could cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It's kind of secret information, but how much it would have helped the Parks Department if it was just half that many police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And that it would have been, they need the money instead of whatever was going on along summer streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And I would just hope that the Parks Department can get more funding and not have an unfunded mandate to check up on things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And thanks a lot.

chapters.summary: Evan Yankee of the Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled lists barriers including inaccessible restrooms, limited travel routes, and poor signage. He supports Intros 212, 1177, and 1193 but says stronger reporting must be backed by funding and stakeholder engagement.
chapters.title: Evan Yankee lists park accessibility barriers and supports bills with funding caveats

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: My name is Evan Yankee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: I'm a 42-year-old white man with shaggy brown hair and a blue suit jacket, and I'm Advocacy Director at Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, an independent living center supporting people with disabilities in Brooklyn and beyond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: When we talk to our members and colleagues with disabilities, we hear over and over again a strong appreciation of New York City's parks and recreation facilities, but we also hear frustration that they are often less accessible than they could and should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: For parks and recreation to meet its mission, access to green space, parks, entertainment must be accessible to all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Currently, people with disabilities face numerous barriers to access in parks, properties, and facilities, including limited access to the full facilities of parks, zoos, beaches, gardens, and recreation facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: A lack of accessible public restrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Barriers of accessible travel to, from, and within park properties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: A lack of accessible information and signage, including accessible navigation information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Safety concerns on pathways and greenways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: And insufficient maintenance of accessible facilities, especially accessible restrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Here are our comments about the bills that the council is considering today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: On Intro 212, we believe this bill is a good step towards remedying some of these problems, but stronger reporting requirements must be backed by sufficient funding and substantial stakeholder engagement with disability groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: City departments are currently required to have a disability service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: facilitator and a five-year accessibility plan, but these interventions have so far fallen short in many departments due to insufficient commitment and a lack of engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Increased funding from the council for the mayor's office for people with disabilities would contribute significantly to the success of these efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: We also support Intro 1177, but ask that it or the Parks Department explicitly clarify that people with disabilities may be accompanied by a personal care assistant for no additional charge at these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: We also strongly support Intro 1193 and urge the Council to consider efforts to make all playgrounds fully accessible, not just the swing sets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: As an independent living center, we work to mobilize the disability community to make their voices heard when decisions are made about the design and operation of parks, properties, and facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: It is our hope that these bills will be followed by a sustained commitment from the city to support this engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: And I'll also add, we appreciated Chair Hanif's questions about the effectiveness of the DSFs and ADA coordinator roles and Councilmember Joseph's questions about agency accessibility plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: In our view, these positions and processes need more resources, staffing, and more of a mandate to make change for people with disabilities at their agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: As our colleague from MOPD pointed out, the ADA is a floor, not a ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: And because most barriers to access only become visible through experience rather than design, getting above that floor involves structured and ongoing engagement with disability communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: and organizations, not just individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: The city should make a commitment to improve these roles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evan Yankee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I'd like to call the second panel, Jonathan Hanen, Lacey Tobert, DJ McDonald, and Simran Bakshi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready.

chapters.summary: Jonathan Hannon, treasurer of Disabled in Action, describes barriers such as fenced grass areas with one opening, narrow walkways with park vehicles, and inaccessible elevated sections of Fort Tryon Park. He also raises unstable beach mats and off-leash dogs as access problems.
chapters.title: Jonathan Hannon details park barriers and lack of agency attentiveness

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Hello, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Well, at this point, just council member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: My name is Jonathan Hannon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I have Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and use a rollator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I'm the treasurer of Disabled in Action and a member of the Accessibility Advisory Committees of the MTA and the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I'm an adjunct lecturer and PhD student at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: As people with disabilities, we experience many difficulties in our daily lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: This includes our access to parks and recreational activities, for which there are many barriers for our access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Many of these issues are known, and the lack of attentiveness of city agencies is concerning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: We shouldn't be an afterthought, but rather valued members of the community, and it's a shame that the entirety of both committees have left before our testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Parks has been detached from the needs of the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: It's a department that has not had its budget even slightly restored to pre-pandemic levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: And while this is not an excuse for their lack of preparation for this hearing, it explains some of our accessibility barriers, but not all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Some are still on their part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: In many city parks, grass areas have short fences surrounding them with only one opening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For people without mobility disabilities, the grass is still easily accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For us, not so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: We need to search like a chicken without a head for the small entrance that others do not need to find.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Think of a large field of grass such as Sheep's Meadow in Central Park where you've had to find the entrance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For people with disabilities, this is our reality for near.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: every field of grass in parks like Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: To add to this, many larger parks have extremely narrow walkways where parks employees drive regularly, expecting pedestrians to get out of the way for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: While most people can easily do so, we as people with disabilities cannot, and we're nearly run off the road.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: To connect this to some of our more elevated parks, such as Fort Tryon Park, where I used to go on ground level daily, there aren't really any ways for us to get to the top for places like the Cloisters or the Lawns, nearly 300 feet in elevation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Most events happen in this elevated portion, and the Park Trust is there as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: This accessibility barrier makes us unable to access the public activities at this park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: To bring other examples, such as the city beaches, there's a two-fold problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: In the summer months, the mobility mats typically aren't stable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: They separate and we have difficulty getting in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Even worse, in the non-summer months, when everybody else can walk on the sand and enjoy themselves, we cannot go with our families to enjoy the sand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: The mats and the beach wheelchairs are only present during beach season, which I understand there's an introduction to be extended, limiting us even further from enjoying the parks of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: As an individual who just moved to Coney Island, I would hope to be able to use the beach just as anyone else can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Finally, I want to emphasize that disability is not only for those of us with mobility disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For example, my wife has a service dog.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: With the abundance of off-leash dogs in parks, she is constantly afraid an off-leash dog will attack her and her son.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: This is a problem that creates barriers to access not only for people with disabilities, but for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: And nothing is done about these off-leash dogs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: This needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: This is but a short list of the many accessibility barriers presented in city parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: These are known issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: In summary, many improvements can be made to increase access to city parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Accessibility should be for all, not just for some.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: And with each barrier we take down, we provide greater access and independence for the community.

chapters.summary: Simran Bakshi, a 15-year-old founder of Speak Up Swing High, says playgrounds are built for children but not every child can enjoy them. She calls for ramps to elevated structures, accessible slides, sensory equipment, and communication boards, not just one adaptive swing.
chapters.title: Simran Bakshi advocates for fully inclusive playgrounds beyond one adaptive swing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Before I begin, I want you to think back to when you were younger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Remember how exciting it was when your parents told you that you can go to the playground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I know that some of my favorite childhood memories were made at my school playground during recess, whether it was jumping off the swings or racing down my friends on a slide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Now, I want you to imagine arriving at that same playground, excited to play, only to realize that almost none of the equipment was assigned for you to use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Sivan Bakshi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I'm a 15-year-old sophomore at Rawson High School and the founder of Speak Up Swing High, a student-led nonprofit working to make playgrounds more inclusive for children with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I started this organization because of my younger brother who has autism and grew up nonverbal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Growing up alongside him opened up my eyes to something I think many people overlook.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Playgrounds are made, are built for children, yet not every child can actually enjoy them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: For many children, playgrounds are places where they can make friends, have fun, and create memories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: But for a child with a disability, something as simple as going down a slide, getting onto a swing, or communicating with another child can be a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: And this issue affects far more families than we may realize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: According to a testimony delivered in May 2026 by the New York City Commissioner for People with Disabilities, Nisha Agarwal,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: More than 1 million New Yorkers live or work in the city with a disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Furthermore, a 2024 audit published by the New York City Comptroller's Office reported disability rates of approximately 10% in Manhattan,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: 15.3% in the Bronx, 10.9% in Brooklyn, 10.3% in Queens, and 10.2% in Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: And while these numbers include people of all ages, they show just how important accessibility is across all the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Yet, when we talk about accessible playgrounds, I think we're often asking the wrong questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Because we typically ask whether a playground is accessible through ramps, paved surfaces, or wheelchair accessible entrances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: What we don't always ask is what a child with a disability can actually do once they get there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I've had conversations with people connected to disability-focused schools and organizations, including the International Academy of Hope, or IHOPE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: And one concern that stood out to me is that even schools serving children with significant disabilities struggle to find playgrounds in their communities of Manhattan where students can fully participate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: And this made me think, what good is a playground with one adaptive swing if that is the only piece of equipment a child can use?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: We need ramps that connect to elevated structures, accessible slides, sensory play equipment, and communication boards that allow children who have difficulty speaking to communicate, interact with others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: We need playgrounds that consider children with physical disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: autism, communication difficulties, and other developmental needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Not just one type of disability and not just one piece of accessible equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Lacey Tauber represents Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso and supports Intro 212. She says Brooklyn has 628 parks but access varies, and the bill would require annual assessments of entrances, bathrooms, playgrounds, beaches, and pools plus a public map.
chapters.title: Lacey Tauber presents Brooklyn Borough President support for Intro 212

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: My name is Lacey Tauber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: I'm a white woman with glasses, blonde hair, and a blue blazer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: I am here representing Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, and we would like to thank Councilmember Honey for co-sponsoring Intro 212 with the Borough President.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: This bill was born out of our comprehensive plan for Brooklyn, which provides a roadmap for long-term equitable growth across the borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: The plan offers a deep analysis of existing inequities in the borough, one of which is access to parks, which has a direct correlation to both physical and mental health outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Brooklyn has 628 parks, though some offer more benefits than others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: New York City Parks Walk to a Park initiative aims to ensure that every New Yorker lives within walking distance of a park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Most of Brooklyn falls within their five-minute walk threshold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: However, a significant number of southern and eastern Brooklynites live 10 minutes or more away from a park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Additionally, this analysis ignores major variations in park size, type of opportunities available, green versus paved space, etc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: There's a map.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: In the testimony that shows access based on NYC Park's threshold of a quarter mile walk and then

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: an updated analysis that accounts for the variations in park typologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Using that analysis, the access gaps become much larger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: But what if you can't walk to a park at all?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: What if you use your mobility device to travel 10 minutes or more to a park only to find that the entrance is obstructed or has stairs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Or you take your child in a wheelchair to the nearest playground only to have to head home because the restroom isn't accessible or the playground lacks inclusive play elements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: While the ADA requires accessibility for all new or materially reconstructed facilities, NYC Parks'five-year accessibility plan notes that the agency has thousands of facilities built prior to the ADA that still need to be made accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: So Intro 212, as we've discussed, would require the agency to conduct an annual assessment of park entrances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Note that entrances would be a new requirement, and this is important given the access issues that I just described, as well as bathrooms, playgrounds, beaches, and pools to determine if they are ADA compliant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: And for those that are not, report on what steps the agency is taking to bring these facilities into compliance and how long it will take to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Additionally, Intro 212 would require NYC Parks to streamline the information that is publicly available about accessible facilities on its website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: To the agency's credit, information about accessible playgrounds, restrooms, and other facilities is available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: However, not all of it is easy to find, and not all of it is in the same place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: The bill would require the agency to create one publicly available map that shows all the information required in the report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Thank you for this issue and your consideration of this legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Borough President Reynoso looks forward to continuing to partner with the Council on improving Brooklyn's parks and making them accessible for everyone.

chapters.summary: DJ McDonald of Dance Parade supports the legislation and supplemental funding. He describes the Cultural Accessibility in New York City project and asks the Disabilities Committee to convene a roundtable on cultural accessibility across city agencies.
chapters.title: DJ McDonald supports bills and proposes cultural accessibility roundtable

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you for receiving my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Introduction and visual description, DJ McDonald, pale-faced male, shaved head and face, wearing black rimmed glasses with blue arms and a bluish sport coat over a black on black

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: striped t-shirt with a small bag at my side and across my chest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: As Grand Marshal Liaison for Dance Parade, who for 20 years has presented its culminating four-hour free

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: to the public dance fest, first in Washington Square, and since year two in Tompkins Square Park, as well as innumerable community engagement programs in both city parks and recreation centers across these years,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: I wish to register my support for the legislation and the resolution introduced at this hearing, as well as adequate supplemental funding, as previous panelists have requested be included.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Dance Parade continues to enjoy a warm and cooperative relationship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: computers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: With both our elected officials,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: and the people of the Parks and Recreation Department, and more frequent support from the Council and oversight of ADA compliance is most welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: I'd also last ask the members of this committee, or the chair, to begin to think of this, and I think you have, beyond simple compliance with the ADA of 1990.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: The 2010 ADA design standards came up in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: As Dance Parade's representative in the weekly Culture at Three and New Yorkers for Culture and Arts Advocacy calls, I also serve as the chair of the steering committee of the Cultural Accessibility in New York City project, CANIC for short,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: a coalition of artists, culture workers, and cultural organizations born as a collaboration between the Disability Justice Accessibility and Collaborative Fundraising Working Groups of Culture 3

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: and funded by New York Community Trust, Ford Foundation, and the Blanche T.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Enders Charitable Trust, the latter of which has renewed its support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: More importantly, the Ford Foundation has granted additional funding through 2028 in support of implementation of our ultimate goal of a sustainable public-private partnership that seeks to ensure ongoing and increased access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: to the cultural riches of the city, including parks, playgrounds, and rec centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: We seek the public part of that partnership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: CANIC offers itself to your committees as we complete within the next weeks our initial research and planning study and prepare to finalize and publish our fundings and recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: My in-person appearance today occurs in pursuance of a reply to our twice-submitted proposal to the Committee on Disabilities through Chair Hannaf,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: especially as a citizen of Council District 39, of a roundtable to examine challenges and opportunities facing us across the cultural landscape and touching agencies and offices that include MOP, DM, MOAM, DCLA,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: including its Create and Place program, New York City Talent, and the Department for the Aging, as well as New York City Parks and Recreations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: I will attach our proposal once again when I submit the written version of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Dance Parade has been proud to have featured Grand Marshals who identify as artists with disabilities in the 20 years of our existence, and I invite all of you to the 21st Parade and Dance Fest on Saturday, May 15th for our 21st iteration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: It would be wonderful to celebrate a creative relationship with the city that exemplifies a more accessible and inclusive landscape in the streets, parks, and playgrounds of our dynamic city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - DJ McDonald
utterances.text: Y'all come.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Even though May is not the month I want to hear about right now.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks Jonathan Hannon about his service on MTA and DOT accessibility advisory committees. Hannon says the DOT committee meets monthly, the MTA quarterly, and both have produced changes like open stroller programs and signage improvements.
chapters.title: Hanif questions Hannon on MTA and DOT accessibility advisory committees

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, Jonathan, you mentioned you...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: serve on the ADA advisory committee, committees for MTA and DOT.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share what happens in these meetings, how frequently you all are meeting?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: So the DOT advisory committee meets approximately once a month and the MTA advisory committee meets approximately once every three months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: In these meetings we discuss pretty much anything that comes up such as accessibility at bus stops, accessibility in the train stations, accessibility on sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Pretty much anything that comes up from the agency gets reported back to these advisory committees for advisory.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Of course, we're just an advisory committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: We can't make any decisions on the matters, but pretty much anything that comes up relating to accessibility, they'll end up bringing it to these committees at some point or another.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so the committee members help inform...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Policy action steps, what deliverables are coming out of the convenings, or is it a venting session?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Typically, these sessions have been more of advising for action, not so much for policy, because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, no policy proposals have come from this to the city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: But in terms of action, a lot of the things that we've advised on these committees have come to fruition, such as on the MTA, there's been the open stroller program on the buses that came out of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: There's been a lot of signage things that came out of the MTA advisory committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: A lot of the things that we're seeing come to fruition lately from these agencies have been in collaboration with these advisory committees.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And who's facilitating the meetings?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is it the disability services facilitator?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: It's typically their disability services facilitator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For the MTA, it's the chief accessibility officer doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For the DOT, it's their ADA coordinator doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: And it's all their departments doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: So their staff are all in these meetings as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: So typically we'll have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: four, five, six representatives from each agency come in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: They might bring in other divisions of the agency, such as at the MTA advisory meetings, we have other divisions of the MTA coming into these meetings to report on matters, such as we've had the Department of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Subways come in, we have had the Department on Buses come in, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: There's been a lot of collaboration coming from those.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And are these meetings typically open to the public?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And are notes broadcasted?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: The MTA meetings are open to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: The DOT meetings are not publicly advertised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I'm not sure about how public access for that is, but that's something that I can look into with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Those advisory committees because I know for the MTA those meetings for the quarterly meetings are publicly posted and the public portions of those meetings that aren't for executive planning are all open to the public including the reports from the other divisions of the MTA.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how did you get involved?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I found out about these by just looking into how advisory, sorry, not advisory, accessibility is on these committees for the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I only found out about it through things like Google.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: In fact, I only found out about joining Disabled in Action after I already joined onto the MTA's advisory committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: It's something that really should be more publicly advertised and it's something that should have more availability to the public to know about rather than just for people who start looking into it and digging for those agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: So the MTA and the DOT as well as Parks, whose advisory committee hasn't met in over six years, that's something that you mentioned that it hasn't met prior to the pandemic, which...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Parks might be able to learn something from how the other agents

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And were you aware that Parks had an inactive ADA advisory committee?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I only found out about that about three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Before that, I didn't even know they had one.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And would you say that the MTA and the DOT committees that you serve on have overlap when it comes to members that serve on those committees?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Very much so that I believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Probably about a third of the committees have overlap, so about a third of the members on each committee serve on the other committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: So it seems like there's need for more public interest in joining these committees, and it seems like we need more voices in the room to be able to make sure that the agencies actually know what needs to be done for the public.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And was this an appointment or did you fill out an application or you expressed interest and then started attending the meetings?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For the DOT, I expressed interest and started attending the meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For the MTA, I applied.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I didn't get on the first time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: I started attending the public meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: And then the second time around, I got onto the committee.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how many committee members are on each?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: For the MTA right now, it's fixed at 15 members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: And for the DOT, I think it can expand as large as the DOT would want it to.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Hannon
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks Simran Bakshi about her organization's adaptive playground equipment work. Bakshi says her group fundraises for equipment and partners with playgrounds on installation, and she criticizes Parks' responses about ADA standards and accessible swings.
chapters.title: Hanif questions Simran Bakshi on adaptive equipment fundraising and Parks response

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: seen your brother experience into real action.

utterances.text: And it's just so meaningful to have someone as young as you come before the committee to testify

utterances.text: have been doing just basic surveying, including speaking to experts like your brothers, caretakers, who serve other families, and then families.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Now, my bill has a similar approach.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's your reaction to how Parks responded?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: From what I heard, based on these different playgrounds, what I see, for example, these playgrounds, they are accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: You can enter these playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: They have done a great job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: You can enter with wheelchairs as well, parking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: There are proper ramps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: But when you get to the playgrounds, there is not much there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I've been to many playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: When I was younger, that's all I'd go to was playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: There's not much there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: How can someone on a wheelchair get onto these elevated structures?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: It's not possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: And I know I think one of the other council members said about having the adaptive swings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: And as I stated during my testimony, adaptive swings are great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: Personally, I focus on stalling them because I had the most knowledge about them because my younger brother had low muscle tone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: So that was something that directly impacted him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: But what is one adaptive swing or two going to do when other kids can't do it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: You do so much more and you're still limited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: There should be playgrounds for children with all abilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: So when there were responses saying about the swings or how they're trying to work with the 2010 ADA standards, I personally don't see it happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Simran Bakshi
utterances.text: I think it's not being facilitated properly.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I look forward to you one day serving as our parks commissioner to get our city on the track that we need it to be.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'd like to call the third panel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Leon Amor Brave, Joe Bellow, William June, Chelton Leggett.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And apologies for mispronouncing your names.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, whenever you're ready, anyone can kick us off.
