utterances.text: Who did we have?

chapters.summary: Shelton Leggett of Trust for Public Land says the organization works to connect people to nature and expand equitable park access. He cites the PS 380K inclusive play demonstration site and the planned Queensway trail, and supports Intro 212.
chapters.title: Shelton Leggett describes Trust for Public Land inclusive playground projects

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Hanif and other members of the Committees on Disabilities and Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: My name is Shelton Leggett, and I am a New York City Playgrounds Program Senior Associate at Trust for Public Land.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Trust for Public Land's mission is to connect people to nature, ensuring that everyone, regardless of ability, has access to the outdoors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Across New York City, we work to expand equitable access to parks, trails, playgrounds, and green spaces for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Numerous studies demonstrate that access to outdoor play and nature reduce stress, increase physical activity, improve mental health, and decreases social isolation among both adults and young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: These benefits make it essential that our public spaces are not only accessible, but also thoughtfully designed to serve people of all abilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: We recently completed work at PS 380K in Williamsburg, which shares a campus with P141K at District 75 school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: This playground serves as a national inclusive play demonstration site.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: This showcases how thoughtfully designed outdoor spaces can create opportunities for children of all abilities to play together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Our commitment to accessibility extends beyond schoolyards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Trust for Public Land is also working with Friends of the Queensway and the City on the Queensway, a proposed trail and linear park along the former Long Island Railroad Rockaway Beach branch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: The Queensway is planned to be fully ADA accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Given the corridor's existing elevated viaducts, bridges, and steep embankments, accessibility is a core consideration in the project's engineering and design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: The first 0.3 mile five acre park is designed to be enjoyed by people of all abilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: These projects reflect Trust for Public Lands'broader commitment to ensuring that accessibility is fundamental to how we plan, design, and build public spaces throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: For these reasons, TPL supports Intro 212, which amends the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Administrative Code of New York City to produce an annual report on compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act standards for accessible design by the Department of Parks and Recreation and to repeal and replace Section

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: 18143 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Accessibility must be an ongoing priority, not an afterthought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: We applaud the Council's efforts to strengthen oversight and reporting in this area and believe this legislation will help move New York City closer to ensuring that all residents, regardless of ability,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: can fully enjoy its parks and public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to address the committee this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: We greatly appreciate your attention to these important issues and look forward to continuing our work toward a more accessible and inclusive New York City.

chapters.summary: William Chen of New York Lawyers for the Public Interest supports Intro 212 but says it should require remediation plans when barriers are identified. He also criticizes new modular bathrooms with 10-minute limits and cell phone or TAC card requirements.
chapters.title: William Chen urges stronger Intro 212 remediation plans and accessible bathrooms

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Hello, my name is William Chen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: I'm a senior staff attorney with the Disability Justice Program and New York Lawyers for the Public Interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair, for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: We have already submitted a testimony together with other disability organizations on today's bills, but today I'll be focusing on strengthening Intro No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: We support the bill, but we believe the bill can be strengthened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: First, the bill should require the Parks Department to actually develop a remediation plan whenever it identifies an accessibility barrier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: As drafted, it only requires reporting on plans that already exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: So we believe the bill can actually require the Parks Department to develop remediation plans when they identify a barrier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Second, the department should consult with people with disabilities and developing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Those plans are important how their feedback was considered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: People with disabilities and disability groups bring first-hand experience that technical assessments may miss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: These improvements

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: are important because people with disabilities still face significant barriers in accessing public parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: For example, the city has proposed adding accessible ramps and gym equipment to the fitness area at Tompkins Square Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Some community members oppose the change, but leaving the area inaccessible should not be the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Accessibility is a legal requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Bathrooms are another serious barrier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Parks hold 77% of the city's public bathrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Yet a city council analysis from last year found that only 58% of public bathrooms citywide are fully accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: And the new bathrooms planned for certain parks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: The mayor's new initiative for putting these modular bathrooms around certain parts of the city, including parks, also repeat these problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: They limit the use of the bathrooms to 10 minutes, after which the doors open automatically, which is a problem for people with disabilities who may need more time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: These bathrooms also require a cell phone or a TAC card, shutting out anyone without one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Other public bathrooms do not impose these requirements, so why are we making it more difficult for these bathrooms that are meant for everyone to use?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: So we therefore urge the council to strengthen Intro 212 so that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: accessibility assessments lead to concrete remediation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Chen
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Joe Bellow, a veterans advocate with NY Metro Vets, supports Intros 212, 1177, 1193, and Res 721. He asks the Council to preserve free recreation center memberships for young adults ages 18 to 24 in Intro 1177.
chapters.title: Joe Bellow supports Intro 1177 and asks to preserve free young adult memberships

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: My name is Joe Bellow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: I'm a veterans advocate and I run a group called NY Metro Vets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: For the record, I support intros 212, 1177, 1193, and RESO 721.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Together, these measures address important aspects of making our parks and recreational resources more accessible, affordable, and inclusive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: As an advocate, I support Intro 1177 in particular because it expands benefits for veterans and active duty military families while making New York City's recreational resources more affordable for New Yorkers of different ages and abilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: As a disabled veteran, I know firsthand that the cost of memberships such as gyms can be a financial barrier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Intro 1177 bills on the local law 18 of 2026 by extending reduced fees beyond recreation centers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: to a much broader range of facilities maintained and operated by the Parks Department, including museums, zoos, wildlife sanctuaries, botanical gardens, and conservation centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: This bill would make reduced annual membership and admission fees available to people age 62 and older, young adults ages 18 to 24, veterans, active duty service members, and the minor children of veterans and active duty service members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: This is meaningful expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: These places are more than attractions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: They are spaces for learning, recreation, family connection, and well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: I do want to raise one concern about the bill in relation to young adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Under the current law, annual memberships at New York City Park Recreation Centers are free for people ages 18 to 24.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: As currently drafted, Intro 1177 removes that expressed statutory guarantee and instead includes young adults among those eligible for reduced fees capped at 25% of the highest applicable fee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: I recognize that New York City Parks'current administrative rules set young adult recreation center memberships at no cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: However, I believe the Council should preserve this benefit explicitly in the law rather than leave it dependent on agency rules that could be changed in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Expanding affordable accessible to more park facilities should not come at the expense of a benefit young adults already have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Therefore, I encourage the sponsors to clarify the language and ensure that free annual recreation center memberships remain protected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: I want to thank Councilmember Shulman, Narcisse, and Marano for their leadership on this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: I also want to recognize the late Edith Prentice, the former president of 504 DEMS, who worked with me to advocate for the 2016 legislation, Local Law 18, and to 504 current president Michael Schweinberg for his support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: I respectfully urge both committees to sign on, support these measures, and move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: move them forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: We took an important step in 2016.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Now is the time to build on that foundation and make sure New York City's parks, recreational facilities are places everyone has the opportunity to enjoy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joe Bellow
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Leona Moore-Brave, a Navy veteran and home health aide, says accessibility is her life because she grew up with siblings with disabilities. She supports Intros 212 and 1177 and calls for real elevators instead of chairlifts and better treatment for home health aides.
chapters.title: Leona Moore-Brave testifies on accessibility, veterans, and home health aides

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Good afternoon, New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all the home health aides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: And good afternoon, chairs and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: My name is Leona Moore-Brave, and I'm a Navy veteran who served as a petty officer, third class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: I noticed speakers today are identifying their race, gender, and uniform, so

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Let me be clear why I'm one of the experts in this room on disability and accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: I'm a biracial woman who grew up in the shadow of Jim Crow laws in Lovingverse, Virginia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: When my existence was barely considered legal, I also grew up with special needs siblings, siblings with intellectual disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Siblings who are deaf and mute, in wheelchairs and on feeding tubes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Accessibility is not policy to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: It is my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: After the Navy, I put on another uniform, maroon scrubs, serving right here as a New York City home health aide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: I'm wearing them today to demand that home health aides finally get the respect and pay they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Too often we are degraded, even though we are the backbone of the medical community, keeping New Yorkers'mothers and children alive every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Scrubs deserve the exact same honor as any military.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Working in these scrubs, I watched amputees get stranded in walk-up apartments without elevators, and I saw firsthand how scary and dangerous navigating New York City in a wheelchair alone is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Even with an aid, it's dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Confining people to cramped apartments causes depression and physical decline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Every human needs parks to stay healthy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: This is why I strongly support...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: 0212 and 1177 for real-time accessibility maps, working park elevators, and affordable public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Above all, New York should not be investing in dangerous, unreliable chairlifts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: We need real elevators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Elevators are straightforward, safe, and essential, not just for the disabled, but for parents carrying babies upstairs where one wrong step could be fatal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Finally, I want to thank New York City for passing the Crown Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: For far too long, Black women have been stigmatized for our hair, told that our natural hair is messy, which kept us locked out of the military and countless other industries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Our hair is Polish, dynamic, and art.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Protecting the right is what true accessibility looks like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: I'm proud to stand with you in making New York accessible for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Leona Moore-Brave
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how Trust for Public Land operates and when it is brought in to build playgrounds. Shelton Leggett says the group works with the School Construction Authority and DEP, and Hanif notes the trust can build faster than city agencies.
chapters.title: Hanif questions Trust for Public Land on schoolyard construction partnerships

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I have a question for Shelton.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the Trust for Public Land operates and when is it brought in to build, help build new playgrounds and parks?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Okay, so I work for the Playgrounds program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: So essentially, our whole job is going into schools, working with students, and then we work with a landscape architect that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: takes their designs and converts it into a finished schoolyard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: So I'm not sure if I answered that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, what I'm trying to get at is, do you all work with the school construction authority?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: And the DEP.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This is funding that's separate from the SEAs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: So the DEP funding is separate from the SCA funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: We have a partnership with the SCA that they essentially will do the project and they reimburse the costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: So it's almost like a, it's like a, it's just a way we learn how to partner that allows us to get projects done and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: have them done efficiently.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Basically, this would be a project of the SCA's.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Why is the trust getting involved?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: That's an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: That's a very interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: I'll have to defer that to maybe like a senior staff member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Our whole program has come about because we figured out how to partner with the city, which is city agencies, in order to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Take these barren spaces that are in school yards and transform them because they're just completely underutilized across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: So we've done about 240 projects and that's helped accessibility for the New York City public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: And so our whole

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: idea, our whole idea in the beginning of this program was to figure out a way to get these

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: spaces flipped and transformed as fast as possible because there just wasn't enough space for children to be playing in like the, you know, mid 80s and

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: No, I deeply appreciate the trust's work and have also worked with you all in my district.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I think the key word here was fast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelton Leggett
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You all are able to step in and do the construction work much faster than our city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We'll now be moving on to the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Gates, Hesu Cove Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready.

chapters.summary: An unnamed public speaker supports Intro 1177 but asks the Council to guarantee free recreation center memberships for residents under 18. The speaker also warns that the bill's young adult language could allow future fees.
chapters.title: Public speaker asks to preserve free rec center memberships for youth

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I strongly support Intro 117's initiative to expand affordable access to recreational facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: However, I believe this legislation presents an opportunity to strengthen existing protections for young New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I believe providing youth with safe, accessible spaces to socialize and exercise is important for crime prevention and should never depend on financial circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Currently, recreation center memberships are free for children under 18 through Parks Department regulations, but while free membership is stated in the Administrative Code for Young Adults, it is not for youth under 18.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Therefore, I request that the Council cement the legal guarantee of free recreation center memberships and other recreational facilities or events for residents under 18 by adding it to Intro 1177.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Secondly, I share the concerns of the previous gentleman who shared regarding the proposed wording for young adults age 18 through 24.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: If I am interpreting the phrase amended to read as follows correctly, intro 1177 will remove the existing provision, guaranteeing free memberships and replace it with a provision that includes young adults among those eligible for discounted fees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Although this does not immediately impose a fee, the change in wording would allow the Parks Department to charge young adults in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I believe this may be an unintended consequence of legislation designed to expand accessibility,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: and therefore propose that the Council amend Intro 1177 to explicitly guarantee free recreational facility access for all individuals ages 24 and younger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hisu Ku Wilson says her daughter Clementine became paralyzed from the waist down after a spinal stroke and now uses a wheelchair. She describes inaccessible brownstone housing and rough hexagonal paths in Prospect Park that make it hard for her daughter to enjoy the park.
chapters.title: Hisu Ku Wilson describes daughter's barriers to Prospect Park after spinal stroke

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Hisu Ku Wilson, and my daughter's name is Clementine Wilson, and she's the reason I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: About a year ago, she was in a freak surfing accident, and she had a spinal stroke, and so she is paralyzed from the waist down at the moment and uses a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And this was about a year ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And since then, we've been in New York, and we have experienced and seen the city in, of course, a completely different way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: I live in Park Slope, and so Clementine has lived there all of her life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: So we live in a brownstone, so she can't come in our house anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: All of our friends and family live in walk-ups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: She's never been able to go inside anyone's house anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: We've rented her an apartment, but one place she should be able to go is the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: You know, and that's the park that she grew up next to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: She went to the tot lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: You know, she ran the turkey trot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: She was a camp counselor at Camp Half-Blood for four years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And last summer we tried to use the park as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And they're very specific things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: For example, just one very specific detail is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: Well, you know, of course you have the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: That's like a ring road.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: That doesn't really...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: mean you're in the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: Now once you enter the park, you know, there is a path, there's a smooth path around the Longmeadow, around Prospect Park West, and it joins up, you know, it winds around, at some point it joins up with an older path.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: That path is made up of concrete hexagonal kind of tiles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And it's kind of, it's worse than cobblestones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: So in effect, you have this long half stretch of the circuit that you could be making that is almost impossible to wheel around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: You know, and that was the same when she was a baby and she was in the, you know, she was in the, you know, the baby chair or, you know, for my parents, you know, we could never go there because they're, you know, they're on, they use canes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: I know that this is just one particular example of something that makes the park inaccessible to her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And I know there are many more, and there are many more issues, there are larger ramifications and projects that you're all dealing with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: But I urge you to also pursue the low-hanging fruit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: The small details as well as the larger scale operations that I know you have to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: And as well as supporting these issues, desperately needs the financial funding, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: Without that, it's meaningless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: So I urge you to please back to pass this bill and do what you...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: Possibly can to make these things

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hisu Ku Wilson
utterances.text: you know, happen and make it possible for my daughter to enjoy the park again, like, as much as she can.

chapters.summary: Hanif thanks Hisu Ku Wilson for advocating for her daughter and for New Yorkers who cannot attend hearings. She says her district team will follow up on local issues and will push Parks on her behalf.
chapters.title: Hanif thanks Hisu Ku Wilson and offers district follow-up

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Hisu, for being here on behalf of your daughter, representing also so many people who can't come out to our hearings on their own.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And it means a lot that you're advocating for her, and by doing that, you're advocating for every New Yorker who is unable to show up today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I want to make sure that we take down your contact since I also happen to represent you as council member and Teyuta and Emmett from my team are here.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We want to just stay in touch following this hearing on just the particular issues that are more local to the 39th Council District.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And we look forward to bugging parks on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Now we will move to a Zoom panel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Chris, Noel, Frankie, Marcial, Kathy Park Price, Evergreen, Arietta.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And we will start with Chris.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Chris Noel, a former Parks accessibility coordinator and wheelchair user, says the biggest obstacle is not identifying inaccessible sites but securing capital funding to fix them. He warns Intro 212 could create an administrative exercise without meaningful improvements.
chapters.title: Former Parks accessibility coordinator Chris Noel says funding is biggest obstacle

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Okay, give me one second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And I'm so happy to be here today as a former park employee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I had the role of accessibility coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So a lot of these issues, I kind of wanted to speak to the parks committee in regards to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: how successful it can be implemented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So let me start with my subject statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I have concerns that the proposed approach for Intro Bill 212 won't necessarily result in more fully accessible ADA-compliant park properties for New Yorkers with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: As someone who uses a manual wheelchair and spent 12 plus years working on these issues inside New York City parks, accessibility has always been a top priority of every employee

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: that walks in the door of a parks property, whether it's a recreation center, whether it's our arsenal building, or any of the buildings that our employees are designated to work out of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I was fortunate enough to help advance the department's accessibility efforts alongside former director, design director Nancy Prince, deputy commissioner Therese Braddock,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: including a development of the New York City Parks Universal Accessibility Design Guidelines, which we put together so that if we aren't in parks anymore, like none of us are, as Nancy Prince and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: former Commissioner Braddock have recently retired, we wanted to make sure that anyone who came in those roles afterwards would be able to follow these strict guidelines to make sure that all parks remain as accessible as they have been.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Having firsthand knowledge of the department's accessibility challenges, I believe the biggest obstacle isn't identifying what's inaccessible, but instead securing the capital funding needed to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: New York City Parks has already

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: invested substantial information documenting these deficiencies provided to the New York State Comptroller's Office after a recent audit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Requiring annual assessments without providing the necessary funding, qualified staffing in this field, and the resources needed to equip them

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: would surely risk creating another administrative exercise without delivering any meaningful improvements to these actual sites for an agency with such a very small budget as New York City Parks have.

chapters.summary: Chris Noel recommends long-term funding commitments from the mayor, Council, and state legislature. He says Parks has less than half a percent of the city budget and suggests each Council member sponsor a playground in their district.
chapters.title: Chris Noel urges 1-2% parks budget and council-sponsored playgrounds

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I'd like to share a few recommendations for a different approach to these bills in front of us today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: One focused on long-term commitment from the mayor, city council members, and the state legislature to actually fund accessibility improvements throughout New York City parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I believe my experience both professionally and personally offer a valuable perspective with these legislations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And the reason I say that is because an intro...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Your time expired.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can keep going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And thank you for allowing me the time because I think I can add a lot of information that wasn't...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Able to be provided prior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Intro 202, it's great, but if we do inspect the playgrounds on an annual basis, meaning parks, you have to have qualified people to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Not everyone knows rise over run or slopes or what type of equipment should be in a playground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So that means parks would

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: have to employ these people or get a consultant, neither of which they have the budget to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I think with parks having less than half of a percent of the city budget is completely ridiculous, especially when you hear the complaints that come year after year about how parks is so inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Parks doesn't have money unless the council or the mayor or assemblyman

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: gives capital dollars to refund a construction of a new park or playground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: That's what it comes down to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I think, if anything, out of this legislative session should come that parks, when we do the city council budget, should be increased at least to 1% or higher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Let's try for 2%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I think every council person should commit to sponsoring a playground in their district every year or every other year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Let's find out if we're doing accounting, let's find out the council people and much respect to the job that you do, who have contributed to funding new park reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: In their districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I give a perfect example of a playground that was constructed in Councilmember Gail Brewer's district, who sponsors many playgrounds in her district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Bloomingdale Playground on West 104th and Amsterdam Playground offers everything that a child with any type of disability would be able to be completely happy in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: We have parks like that that are being constructed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: A lot of, as the 15-year-old advocate, who I very much say she presents,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: into the cell very well in her statement, you can go inside of most parks, but when it comes to the play equipment, that's old and outdated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So it's not like you're going to just replace the play equipment and leave the rest of the park as it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: It requires a full capital reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Parks doesn't have the money to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So as many people that might complain and say, hey, all of our parks aren't accessible, we have to look at who's funding them.

chapters.summary: Chris Noel asks how zoos and museums would verify disability for reduced memberships under Intro 1177. He says Parks uses pre-qualifying documents like MTA half-fare cards, DOT placards, and Access-A-Ride cards.
chapters.title: Chris Noel raises disability verification concerns for Intro 1177

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: In terms of Intro 1177, I do have a question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: It talks about discounted memberships, as Parks already does for people with disabilities, veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: It's free for children under 18.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: But the question I have is, if you're looking to have museums or zoos to reduce their membership, they already do for seniors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: But for people with disabilities, as Parks came into this problem as well, it's identifying a person's disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So what Parks does is they say, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Let's get something where your disability has already been defined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So we say, okay, get an MTA half-fair metro card, get a DOT placard, you know, get an accessor ride card.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Because those agencies already do the, I guess, background research to determine if a person is disabled or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So for parks, it made it more accessible for our staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: To let people in with disabilities or to qualify them for disabled membership because they already had that pre-qualification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: have a zoo or a museum or anything on parks land to kind of identify what qualifies as a person with disability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: would be a huge task unless they do what we do in our recreation centers where you have to bring one of those required documents from an accredited

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: edited city or state agency.

chapters.summary: Chris Noel supports Intro 1193 in principle but says replacing conventional swings with ADA swings can require removing two swings for one. He says new construction already requires accessible swings for different age groups.
chapters.title: Chris Noel says accessible swing installation requires site-specific tradeoffs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: In regards to intro 1193, I do agree that all parks should have ADA swings for two to five and five to 12.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And then it is that isn't a design guidelines for newly constructed playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: If we were to say, take out the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: bucket swings, which are two to five, or the strap swings, which are usually for five to 12.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Sometimes that means we have to take out two of those swings for one ADA swing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: A lot of times that causes discomfort with the community who says, hey, you took out two swings for one, even though we're providing more accessibility with that ADA swing, which are pretty cool and everyone loves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: It comes a problem of do we take away swings for one?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So at each site would kind of be a different situation or scenario.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So even though I do agree with the bill, how easily it can be accomplished is another question because of the existing site conditions and the swing bays that the swings are currently in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: To replace those swings with an ADA swing isn't as easy as it seems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: But as the former accessibility slash DSF coordinator, DSF associate was, there were times where people called in and requested a specific ADA swing for their park and playground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And we forwarded that to the chief of operations for that borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And we did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Try to accommodate them, whereas if it was possible, even if it meant taking out two swings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So it can be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I just think there needs to be a little bit more direction on if you're trying to put them in every swing bay and you're eliminating other swings, meaning the two for one swap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: In new construction, it's already required for a 5 to 12 and a 2 to 5 ADA swing with the addition of the buckets and an addition of the strap swings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So that's my comments today.

chapters.summary: Chris Noel says he handled three positions at once and praises current DSF Rain Credo, Rodolfo Rivera, and ADA coordinator Edmund Asirio. He says Parks needs a higher budget and more investment from city and state officials.
chapters.title: Chris Noel praises Parks DSF staff and calls for more funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I'd really like to talk to your office in regards to this, these bills, because as a former parky, I was the one getting the complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And I believe everyone in that room who has dealt, who has sent a disability related complaint to parks, they've talked to me about it and we resolved it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And it's being completely done, I believe, that way by our new DSF reign, as well as Rodolfo Rivera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And Edmund Desirio, who's in capital projects as the accessibility coordinator, is doing a remarkable job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: You got to understand, I was doing three positions at one time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So now that we're spread out into three separate positions, I think it will still be a great task for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: But I believe they're doing a great job in my absence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: One last thing I would say before I go, and not to take too much time, but it's just because I hear so many complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And I was on the other side in terms of a parky.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I look at it as a small budgeted city agency getting a lot of complaints and don't have the money or funding to correct it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I think that needs to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I think parks needs a higher budget than half of 1%, which is completely ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And there needs to be more investment from the city council members, the mayor, and the assembly who have capital dollars to extend to these projects and make them more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So I think it requires further conversation for a lot of these intros.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I'm in favor of intro, my personal opinion, intro 1193, if it can be done adequately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I'm in favor of intro 1177, if it can be done adequately, meaning a zoo or a museum would be able to know how to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: differentiate someone who says they have a disability from someone who really does to get that discounted membership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And that's something we went through with Parks when we discounted our membership to $25 for people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: And for Intro 212, I think it's, I don't think it's really going to move the needle in terms of getting our parks more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: We can easily say, hey, these parks aren't accessible year after year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: They're still not going to be accessible without funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: So are we spinning the wheel trying to give the public and the council as much information?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: on how inaccessible our parks are annually?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Or are we looking at how many parks can the city council, the mayor and assembly fund annually?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: I've gone way over my time, so I thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We appreciate your invaluable concerns and questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Frankie, Marcelle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Frankie Ann Marcel, a vision rehabilitation therapist and legally blind mother, says inaccessible signage, inconsistent pathways, and poor contrast create barriers. She calls for braille boards, tactile and high-contrast signage, and inclusive programming as standard design.
chapters.title: Frankie Ann Marcel calls for tactile signage and inclusive design for blind New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Can everyone hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: My name is Frankie Ann Marcel, and I'm a vision rehabilitation therapist and orientation and mobility specialist at Vision Services for the Blind and Visually Impaired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: I am also legally blind myself and a mother to a toddler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: For 100 years, Visions has served blind and low vision New Yorkers across all five boroughs, providing free rehabilitation services that empower individuals of all ages to live independently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: We teach skills ranging from independent travel and daily living to assistive technology and community participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: As a rehabilitation professional, I teach individuals to navigate their environment safely and independently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: But independence is not achieved through rehabilitation alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: The environments we navigate must also be accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Parks, playgrounds, and recreation centers are essential spaces for socialization and community connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Yet inaccessible signage, inconsistent pathways, poor contrast,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: and limited accessible programming create barriers for individuals with vision loss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: As a mother with low vision, I spend many weekend days at the playground and have experienced how meaningful inclusive design can be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Visiting playgrounds with braille alphabet boards built into the play structure has allowed me to share an accessible learning experience with my child.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Knowing that this design element was made for children with vision loss and for parents with vision loss like myself to engage with such an empowering and meaningful experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: But it shouldn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: These inclusive aspects of universal design should be so common that they are considered the norm, just as a print alphabet board is for a person or a child with sight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: And that can start right here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Accessibility is not simply about getting into a space, it is about being able to fully experience it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: We need accessible pathways, tactile and high contrast signage, inclusive equipment and programming that welcomes everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: At Visions, we teach people the skills to navigate the world independently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: We need the city to ensure that the world we are teaching them to navigate is accessible as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Every New Yorker deserves the opportunity to play, explore, exercise, and connect with their community safely, independently, and with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frankie Ann Marcel
utterances.text: Thank you all so much for the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Noel
utterances.text: Kathy Park-Brice.

chapters.summary: Kathy Park Price of New Yorkers for Parks supports Intros 212 and 1193 but says they must be paired with funding. She says ADA compliance is the floor and calls for at least 1% of the city budget for parks.
chapters.title: Kathy Park Price supports bills but says parks need full funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon, Chair Hanif and members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hanif and Chair Hankerson for holding this important hearing and bringing our attention to the issues of accessibility in our park system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: The issues don't receive enough attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: I'm Kathy Park Price, Director of Advocacy and Policy at New Yorkers for Parks, a citywide nonprofit that fights for high quality parks and open space for every New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We also help lead the Playfair for Parks Coalition, made up of more than 450 organizations advocating for fully funding our park system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Hanif and Hankerson, for supporting our call to dedicate at least 1% of the city's budget to parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And we also heard at least two other testimonies calling for 1% for parks today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We support Councilmember Hanif's Intro 212, developed in partnership with Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, as well as Councilmember Marte's Intro 1193 to expand accessible swings in playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We see these bills as important steps toward a more accessible park system, but they must be accompanied by the funding needed to deliver meaningful improvements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: across the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And I think we can agree that making our parks accessible to all New Yorkers is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We can also agree that New York City Parks has made important progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We also recognize that there are challenges to updating a very old system and old infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And so I think about what one of the parks representatives said today, and that's ADA compliance or ADA is the floor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And for that reason, I want to focus my testimony on a couple of solutions.

chapters.summary: Kathy Park Price notes Parks has vacant capital team positions and says project managers are needed to deliver accessibility projects. She says accessibility also depends on operating funds for clean bathrooms, repairs, and extended facility hours.
chapters.title: Kathy Park Price says accessibility is also a capital staffing and operating budget issue

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We heard about significant capital achievements in accessibility, including the beautiful new Shirley Chisholm Rec Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: But we also heard Parks say that they have vacancies on its capital team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And when we talk about that, we're talking about project managers, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Last year, New Yorkers for Parks called for restoring 59 capital team positions that we know are vacant and adding more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And those were in our FY27 budget recommendations to help unlock the nearly $450 million installed capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So when we talk about capital, we're not only talking about building, but we're talking about the people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Project managing these projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And so

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So a fully funded park system also addresses that need, that accessibility need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So accessibility is also an operating budget issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: It's about keeping our bathrooms open and clean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Going.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You can keep going, Kathy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Keeping repairing broken pavement, maintaining playgrounds and rec centers, and extending facility hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And these are things that require staff and sustained funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And accessibility can also take other...

chapters.summary: Kathy Park Price says New Yorkers for Parks and Transportation Alternatives are campaigning to reduce personal vehicles in parks. She also proposes a comprehensive long-term strategic plan for parks, similar to DOT's streets plan, to ensure accountability across administrations.
chapters.title: Kathy Park Price proposes car-free parks and long-term strategic plan

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Forms and we encourage parks to take a leadership role in developing ways to other ways to address accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So for example, we heard a few minutes ago from a disability advocate saying

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: they have to dodge vehicles in our parks and I want to note that New Yorkers for Parks and Transportation Alternatives is leading a campaign to reduce and eliminate personal vehicles from our parks and people can read more about that at bit.ly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: slash carfree parks nyc all lowercase

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We also heard today parks acknowledge that limited resources constrain its ability to improve accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So that was an important acknowledgement and an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So what additional resources does parks need?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: How has the administration responded?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: With a mayor committed to investing 1% of the city's budget,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: to parks, we should be identifying those needs and funding them in FY28.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Everyone on the Parks and Disability Committees can now follow up on this issue, on this to ensure that whatever parks needs to make our park system more accessible is funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Finally, Chair Hankerson raised an important question about how to maintain progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: As administrations and priorities change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: One answer is, or idea, is a comprehensive long-term strategic plan for parks, much like DOT's streets plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: What is the agency's long-term vision for a truly world-class park system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: What investment, staffing, milestones will get us there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: A plan could address the transparency and accountability needs that we've talked about today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: And the parks has many different plans out there, waterfront plans and climate or the urban forest plan, for example, but a comprehensive strategic plan would be beneficial.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: So we support these bills because better information and stronger accountability are essential, but ultimately we need to pair those with those commitments with the resources and long-term vision to deliver them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: We cannot have a truly accessible park system without a fully funded park system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kathy Park Price
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Evergreen Arrieta, a disabled Rockaway resident, says she assessed four ADA beach entrances this summer and none were wheelchair accessible. She calls for better MobiMat maintenance, signage, 311 reporting, and expanded beach wheelchair access beyond the swimming season.
chapters.title: Evergreen Arrieta describes broken beach mats and need for maintenance funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: This meeting was so long that my iPad is at 5%, even though I have it plugged in, so I hope it doesn't die.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: My name is Evergreen Arrieta.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I am a disabled resident of Farrakhoy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I am an indigenous person with black hair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I am here to ask for reformation of Parks'movie mat maintenance policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I just listened to staffs park say that movie mats are quick to fix.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I visited and assessed four different ADA entrances this summer, and none of them were wheelchair accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I have to send someone ahead of me to check if the mats are clear to avoid fatigue and disappointment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: This denies me independence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Fixing a mat is exhausting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: It requires constant communication with parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: And in my experience, the amazing support of Councilmember Brooks Powers'office supported me to get it done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: This summer, more than 10 people helped to get me onto the beach, and two mats were repaired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: These people saved my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: To better plan a beach visit, please increase funding for maintenance workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Parks must provide a regular maintenance schedule, transparency about how maintenance happens, more signage, public information about which mats

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: are ADA compliant, there's 14 of them, but every single entrance that I have been to has a blue mat, so it's highly confusing which are the 14 that a wheelchair can safely cross.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I've lived here six years and I only learned this this summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: My community has discovered that many of the entrances are incorrectly listed online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: As a result, in July, the first national database on beach accessibility launched with outdated parks information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: The inability to plan is a heartbreaking barrier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: It's unacceptable that there's no simple way to report a blue mat needing repair on 311.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: It redirects you to make a human rights complaint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: One of the biggest barriers is the original installment of the mats in May.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: If there's sand or gaps left between the mat and the concrete, that whole magical runway is useless to a wheelchair user.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Please have more oversight of Moby Mat installment by like experts that other people mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: The beach itself is only ADA compliant from Memorial Day to Labor Day, and that window is cut short because of poor maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I lost five weeks of the summer season, and it was so short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: That really hurt me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: There needs to be a conversation about uncoupling parks, beach wheelchair access, and the rentals to just the swimming season to expand access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Today is beautiful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I have it right here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I can see it outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: If that was available online, I think it's shut down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I understand that people cannot swim anymore, so it's no longer offered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: But what if you just want to go on the sand?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Lastly, I want to highlight Beach 17th as one of the most accessible entrances that I have visited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I provided photos and recommendations when I signed up to include piloting a beach walker rental at Beach 17th because it's regularly used by seniors with walkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: That entrance is a dream come true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: It even has railings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: It should be replicated across all of the 14 parks entrances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I'd love to know when it's going to happen and who's going to give the money for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: I know that getting Medicaid to repair a walker that's damaged by sand is a nightmare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: So beach walkers would radically improve the lives of many people here in Rockaway and citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: And they're very inexpensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: There is a huge culture of volunteerism and beach programming in summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: In Rockaway, disabled people are largely left out because of the lack of beach access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: And if there's a dune restoration volunteer day, can there be a Moby Mat restoration volunteer day?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Rockaway is ready and willing to help, but we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: We need to be mobilized by someone, anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: This hearing has left me wondering, can a nonprofit make a reasonable accommodation for events at the beach?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Evergreen Arrieta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sherry Yvette Barnett says she came to speak with Chair Hanif about her daughter's passing and previous attempts to reach her office. Hanif offers follow-up with her team and asks to continue the hearing.
chapters.title: Sherry Yvette Barnett raises personal grievance during public testimony

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shahana Hanif.

utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is out of current hearing protocol.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So if you'd like to testimony on the topic covered today, I'm happy to give you the time.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And if you'd like to talk to somebody on my team, Teyuta and Emmett,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We'll follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: I'll give you two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett
utterances.text: That's why I came here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sherry Yvette Barnett

summary: Committee on Disabilities and Parks and Recreation held a joint oversight hearing on accessibility of city parks, playgrounds, and recreation centers.
Parks officials testified about the ADA transition plan, capital projects, staffing, and concerns with Intros 212, 1177, and 1193.
Public testimony from disability advocates, service providers, and residents described persistent barriers and called for more funding and accountability.
